The barrier is institutional design. Global leaderboards do not include these benchmarks, and no governance mechanism compels them to do so. Commercial pressure corrects leaderboard failures when paying customers in the Global North are affected. The Global South lacks equivalent leverage. Without governance, failures affecting Hindi, Swahili, or Arabic speakers persist indefinitely as documented but unaddressed gaps. Using India as a case study (1.4 billion people, 22 scheduled languages, high-quality benchmarks, but no trusted aggregation), we report findings from a consultation with 58 AI practitioners showing consistent preference for formal governance and disclosure-based conflict management. The solution is not more data but better institutions: regional leaderboards with independent governance from the start.

AI.tldr: AI leaderboards systematically exclude Global South languages due to institutional design failures, not data gaps; independent governance for regional benchmarks is needed.
AI.motivation: Current AI leaderboards are structurally biased against the Global South, excluding high-quality regional benchmarks for languages like Hindi, Swahili, and Arabic, perpetuating documented but unaddressed gaps.
AI.method: Analyzes institutional design flaws in global leaderboards, uses India as case study (1.4B people, 22 languages), and reports findings from consultation with 58 AI practitioners.
AI.result: Practitioners consistently prefer formal governance and disclosure-based conflict management; reveals commercial pressures only correct leaderboard failures affecting Global North customers.
AI.conclusion: Solution is not more data but better institutions: regional leaderboards with independent governance from the start to serve Global South populations effectively.

title: ClosureBench: A Constructive Benchmark for Compositional Graph Reasoning
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/egolabs-ai/closurebench
summary:
We introduce ClosureBench, a constructive benchmark for compositional graph-relational reasoning with programmatically verified ground truth. Unlike fixed-test-set benchmarks vulnerable to data contamination, ClosureBench generates instances on demand: each task's reference answer is computed by executing a program in the Ein tensor-logic language, ensuring machine-verified correctness. The benchmark spans 26 task categories at three compositional levels (L1-L3), with difficulty controlled along three independent axes: graph size, edge density, and query depth.
  We evaluate models from 1.5B open weights to frontier systems (o3, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5, Claude Sonnet 4) and report three findings. First, because the benchmark can always supply fresh instances, it measures memorisation directly: a model fine-tuned on a fixed test set shows a 19.3 percentage-point gap between its accuracy on seen and on fresh instances, which a static test set cannot reveal. We scope this to supervised fine-tuning on answer pairs, not pretraining contamination. Second, accuracy falls as graph size and query depth increase, and the two interact: models misread the graph from its natural-language description and then reason correctly over the wrong graph, so even the strongest frontier model degrades from atomic to compositional queries. This bottleneck is a property of the reasoning rather than the input format: it persists when the graph is given as a JSON edge list or an adjacency matrix instead of prose. Third, a 4B model fine-tuned to emit executable programs rather than answers stays nearly flat across compositional levels and approaches frontier accuracy (94.3% on held-out instances) at a fraction of the token cost. This holds for two program targets, Ein and Python+NetworkX, so it is a property of verified program synthesis rather than of one language.

AI.tldr: ClosureBench is a dynamic benchmark for graph reasoning with programmatically verified answers, revealing memorization issues, reasoning bottlenecks with increasing complexity, and superior performance from program-synthesis models.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks have fixed test sets vulnerable to data contamination, making it hard to distinguish memorization from genuine reasoning. There's a need for benchmarks with verified ground truth that can generate fresh instances on demand to properly evaluate compositional graph-relational reasoning.
AI.method: ClosureBench generates instances programmatically using the Ein tensor-logic language, ensuring machine-verified correctness. It spans 26 task categories across three compositional levels (L1-L3) with difficulty controlled by graph size, edge density, and query depth. The benchmark evaluates models from 1.5B to frontier systems and compares traditional answer generation with program synthesis approaches.
AI.result: Three key findings: 1) A 19.3% accuracy gap between seen and fresh instances reveals memorization in fine-tuned models. 2) Accuracy drops with graph size/query depth increase due to models misreading graph descriptions. 3) A 4B model fine-tuned for program synthesis maintains near-flat performance across compositional levels, achieving 94.3% accuracy with much lower token cost.
AI.conclusion: Program synthesis with verified execution outperforms direct answer generation for compositional reasoning tasks, suggesting that the bottleneck lies in understanding graph descriptions rather than reasoning itself. Dynamic benchmarks like ClosureBench are essential for revealing true model capabilities beyond memorization.

title: Safety Alignment Illusion: The Cross-Lingual Safety Gap in LLMs
comment: 7 pages, 8 figures, submitted to IEEE SLT (Spoken Language Technology) 2026
summary: Current safety alignment training for Large Language Models (LLMs) are heavily English-centric. When such safety filters fail for non-English languages, the consequences are immediate and user-facing: voice assistants and spoken dialogue systems may produce stereotype-reinforcing outputs, bypassing the standard English-focused safety alignments and propagating harmful bias to non-English speaking communities. For spoken language technologies deployed across India's linguistically diverse population, this represents a critical failure mode. To address this cross-lingual gap, we introduce INCLUDE (Indian Cultural Lens for Understanding and Detecting Embedded Biases), a multilingual evaluation benchmark designed to quantify Indian-centric socio-cultural biases. INCLUDE consists of 2,604 prompts spanning six prompt languages: English, Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, and Hinglish (Hindi-English code-mix). We evaluate ten open- and closed-source LLMs against this benchmark, analyzing 14,988 bias scores. Our statistical results reveal two key findings. First, Bengali yielded the highest average bias score in open-source models. Second, English demonstrated a notable reversal, producing the lowest bias in open-source models but the highest bias in closed-source models.

AI.tldr: INCLUDE benchmark reveals significant safety alignment gaps for Indian languages in LLMs, showing concerning cross-lingual bias disparities between open- and closed-source models.
AI.motivation: Current safety alignment training for LLMs is heavily English-centric, creating critical failure modes when deployed in linguistically diverse regions like India. When safety filters fail for non-English languages, voice assistants and spoken dialogue systems can produce stereotype-reinforcing outputs that bypass standard English-focused alignments and propagate harmful bias to non-English speaking communities.
AI.method: The authors introduce INCLUDE (Indian Cultural Lens for Understanding and Detecting Embedded Biases), a multilingual evaluation benchmark designed to quantify Indian-centric socio-cultural biases. INCLUDE consists of 2,604 prompts spanning six prompt languages: English, Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, and Hinglish (Hindi-English code-mix). They evaluate ten open- and closed-source LLMs against this benchmark, analyzing 14,988 bias scores.
AI.result: Statistical results reveal two key findings: (1) Bengali yielded the highest average bias score in open-source models, and (2) English demonstrated a notable reversal, producing the lowest bias in open-source models but the highest bias in closed-source models.
AI.conclusion: There are significant cross-lingual gaps in LLM safety alignment, particularly for Indian languages, highlighting the need for multilingual safety training and evaluation benchmarks like INCLUDE to address bias propagation to non-English speaking communities.

title: Bidirectional representational alignment between biological and artificial neural networks
summary: Recent work has shown that representational alignment between biological and artificial neural networks is asymmetric: model representations predict neural responses much better than neural responses predict model representations. This asymmetry raises the question of whether representational geometry contributes to bidirectional representational alignment. We hypothesized that steering representational geometry during training can systematically influence bidirectional alignment. To test this hypothesis, we developed a computational framework that integrates spectral regularization with bidirectional predictivity analyses. As an initial demonstration, we evaluated our framework using self-supervised contrastive vision models. Steering the spectral geometry of the learned representations substantially increased reverse predictivity with modest reductions in forward predictivity, yielding a 55% relative improvement in bidirectional predictivity. These improvements were accompanied by reduced effective dimensionality and a reorganization of the shared representational subspace, within which forward and reverse predictivity became approximately symmetric at intermediate spectral exponents. Overall, these findings demonstrate that representational geometry can be systematically steered to modulate bidirectional representational alignment between biological and artificial neural networks.

AI.tldr: Steering representational geometry during training improves bidirectional alignment between biological and artificial neural networks by 55%, making forward and reverse predictivity more symmetric.
AI.motivation: Previous research shows representational alignment between biological and artificial neural networks is asymmetric (models predict neural responses much better than vice versa), raising the question of whether representational geometry contributes to bidirectional alignment.
AI.method: Developed a computational framework integrating spectral regularization with bidirectional predictivity analyses. Used self-supervised contrastive vision models as initial demonstration, steering spectral geometry of learned representations during training.
AI.result: Steering spectral geometry substantially increased reverse predictivity with modest reductions in forward predictivity, yielding 55% relative improvement in bidirectional predictivity. Improvements accompanied by reduced effective dimensionality and reorganization of shared representational subspace, where forward and reverse predictivity became approximately symmetric at intermediate spectral exponents.
AI.conclusion: Representational geometry can be systematically steered to modulate bidirectional representational alignment between biological and artificial neural networks.

title: Optimized Fuzzy Logic Approach with the IEEE Key Gas Method for Diagnosing Power Transformer Faults Using Dissolved Gas Analysis
comment: This paper was presented at 2025 10th International Conference on Applying New Technology in Green Buildings (ATiGB). Please cite the published version
summary: Reliable transformer fault diagnosis is essential for maintaining power system stability. The IEEE Key Gas Method (KGM), a widely utilized approach in Dissolved Gas Analysis (DGA), exhibits limitations in addressing ambiguous data and ensuring high diagnostic accuracy. This study presents An enhanced model combining Fuzzy Logic with the IEEE Key Gas Method (FL-KGM) that introduces refined membership functions, optimized fuzzy rule sets, and a novel separation of CO and CO2 to eliminate diagnostic inconsistencies. By leveraging multidimensional gas ratio analysis and an adaptive classification framework, FL-KGM delivers superior fault identification and classification. Experimental validation utilizing real-world datasets demonstrates that FL-KGM achieves up to 98.6% accuracy, significantly outperforming KGM and other FL-based approaches. These findings elucidate the potential of FL-KGM in advancing transformer monitoring, enabling intelligent fault detection, and enhancing predictive maintenance strategies in modern power systems.

AI.tldr: FL-KGM combines fuzzy logic with IEEE Key Gas Method to improve transformer fault diagnosis accuracy to 98.6%, outperforming existing methods by addressing ambiguous data and diagnostic inconsistencies.
AI.motivation: The IEEE Key Gas Method (KGM) used in transformer Dissolved Gas Analysis has limitations in handling ambiguous data and achieving high diagnostic accuracy, necessitating an enhanced approach for more reliable transformer fault diagnosis in power systems.
AI.method: Enhanced model combining Fuzzy Logic with IEEE Key Gas Method (FL-KGM) featuring refined membership functions, optimized fuzzy rule sets, novel separation of CO and CO2 gases, multidimensional gas ratio analysis, and an adaptive classification framework.
AI.result: FL-KGM achieves up to 98.6% accuracy in fault identification and classification, significantly outperforming the standard KGM and other fuzzy logic-based approaches when validated on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: FL-KGM demonstrates substantial potential for advancing transformer monitoring, enabling intelligent fault detection, and enhancing predictive maintenance strategies in modern power systems through superior diagnostic performance.

title: SIGMA: Symmetry-aware, Intelligent, Geometric, Multi-objective Adaptive Control for Robust, Dependable Traffic Management
summary: Traffic signal control is a complex sequential decision-making problem requiring real-time adaptation and trade-offs among throughput, delay fairness, signal stability, and emergency vehicle priority. Existing RL methods often fix objectives, ignore dynamic priority changes, and fail to generalize across geometrically similar intersections.We propose SIGMA (Symmetry-aware, Intelligent, Geometric, Multi-objective Adaptive traffic control), an RL framework enhanced with a large language model (LLM) for adaptive objective tuning and orientation-invariant learning. SIGMA converts natural-language emergency commands into priority vectors for a multi-objective actor-critic controller, avoiding manual reward engineering. Rotational augmentation improves transferability across four-way intersections, while offline-to-online learning ensures stable initialization and gradual adaptation to changing traffic.We define reliability properties covering emergency service levels, graceful degradation under LLM failures, and demand sensitivity, validated via bootstrap statistics. Evaluated in SUMO on four Kolkata-based urban intersections against fixed-time, actuated, and DQN controllers, SIGMA reduces average/emergency waiting times and queue lengths, and boosts throughput. Ablation studies confirm robustness to component failures and geometric rotations. Overall, SIGMA offers a reliable, language-guided, multi-objective traffic control system with statistical reliability assurance.

AI.tldr: SIGMA is an RL framework for traffic signal control that uses LLMs for adaptive objective tuning and orientation-invariant learning, with proven performance improvements and reliability assurances.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for traffic signal control have limitations: they fix objectives, ignore dynamic priority changes, fail to generalize across geometrically similar intersections, and require manual reward engineering.
AI.method: SIGMA combines LLMs with multi-objective actor-critic RL, converts natural-language emergency commands into priority vectors, uses rotational augmentation for transferability, and employs offline-to-online learning for stable initialization and adaptation.
AI.result: SIGMA reduces average/emergency waiting times and queue lengths, boosts throughput compared to fixed-time, actuated, and DQN controllers, and shows robustness to component failures and geometric rotations through ablation studies.
AI.conclusion: SIGMA offers a reliable, language-guided, multi-objective traffic control system with statistical reliability assurance and improved performance over existing methods.

title: Improving Rural Medication Safety with AI: A Scoping Review
summary:
Introduction: Medication errors (MEs) represent a significant threat to global healthcare systems, contributing to patient harm. Introducing artificial intelligence (AI) in rural healthcare enhances patient safety. The aim is to explore the applications and effectiveness of AI technologies in enhancing patient safety and reducing medication errors in rural health settings.
  Methods: A scoping review was conducted through a systematic literature search spanning 2012 to 2025 across multiple databases, including EBSCohost, Emcare (Ovid), MEDLINE, and the ProQuest Consumer Health Database. Twelve primary studies from nine different nations were examined. Data were analysed thematically to obtain insights on AI interventions across the medication process.
  Results: AI technologies have been integrated into every stage of medication management, right from prescribing and dispensing to administration and post-administration monitoring. Four key themes came to light: (1) the various types of AI being utilised (like Clinical Decision Support Systems, Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing, and smart pumps); (2) the phases of the medication process that are affected; (3) how effective these technologies are in minimising errors and boosting workflow safety; and (4) rural-specific challenges including infrastructure, staff training, system integration, and alert fatigue. Several studies have demonstrated that machine learning-based surveillance improves incident detection and reduces prescribing and transcription errors by an impressive 34% to 80%. Barriers included lack of governance frameworks, financial limitations, and clinician resistance, which still present major obstacles.
  Conclusion: In rural healthcare, AI technologies hold great potential for enhancing pharmaceutical safety. They can allow data-driven monitoring, automate processes, and offer clinical decision assistance.

AI.tldr: This scoping review explores how AI technologies (CDSS, ML, NLP, smart pumps) can reduce medication errors and improve patient safety in rural healthcare settings, identifying both effectiveness (34-80% error reduction) and implementation challenges.
AI.motivation: Medication errors represent a significant threat to global healthcare, particularly in rural settings where resources are limited. There's a need to explore how artificial intelligence can enhance patient safety and reduce medication errors in these underserved areas.
AI.method: A scoping review was conducted through systematic literature search (2012-2025) across multiple databases (EBSCohost, Emcare, MEDLINE, ProQuest Consumer Health Database). Twelve primary studies from nine nations were analyzed thematically to examine AI interventions across medication processes.
AI.result: AI technologies are integrated throughout medication management stages (prescribing, dispensing, administration, monitoring). Key findings include: 1) Types of AI used (CDSS, ML, NLP, smart pumps), 2) Affected medication process phases, 3) Effectiveness in reducing errors (ML-based surveillance showed 34-80% reduction in prescribing/transcription errors), and 4) Rural-specific challenges (infrastructure, training, integration, alert fatigue).
AI.conclusion: AI technologies show great potential for enhancing pharmaceutical safety in rural healthcare through data-driven monitoring, process automation, and clinical decision support. However, barriers like governance frameworks, financial limitations, and clinician resistance must be addressed for successful implementation.

title: Rethinking Privileged Information in On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on its own responses using token-level supervision from the same model conditioned on privileged reference information. We investigate whether performance gains from OPSD show that the student learned the information in the reference or instead reflect recovery of reasoning behavior already present in the base model. We perform OPSD experiments on science and mathematics datasets using Qwen3 models ranging from 1.7B to 8B. Our analysis framework separates the supervision induced by the reference from the supervision provided by the teacher without the reference and measures how each aligns with changes in the student's predictions. The correct reference does not provide a consistent performance benefit across teacher generation modes, model sizes, and training datasets. Students can improve without the correct reference, and a solution from another problem can outperform the correct solution on several mathematical reasoning benchmarks. The student's predictions align more strongly with the base model's thinking behavior than with the supervision induced by the reference, but controls constructed from other problems reproduce much of both alignments. Moreover, stronger alignment attributable to the correct reference does not reliably coincide with a greater performance benefit from the reference. Performance gains and distributional alignment alone therefore cannot determine how privileged reference information contributes to student learning in OPSD.

AI.tldr: OPSD performance gains don't necessarily mean students learn reference information; improvements often come from recovering existing reasoning patterns rather than learning from privileged references.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether performance gains from On-policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) actually reflect learning of privileged reference information or simply recovery of reasoning behavior already present in the base model.
AI.method: Used analysis framework that separates supervision from references vs. supervision from teachers without references; tested on science and math datasets using Qwen3 models (1.7B-8B); examined alignment between student predictions and base model thinking behavior vs. reference-induced supervision.
AI.result: Correct references don't consistently benefit performance; students can improve without correct references; solutions from other problems can outperform correct solutions on math reasoning benchmarks; student predictions align more with base model thinking than reference supervision; stronger reference alignment doesn't reliably correlate with performance benefits.
AI.conclusion: Performance gains and distributional alignment alone cannot determine how privileged reference information contributes to student learning in OPSD; improvements often reflect recovery of existing reasoning patterns rather than learning from references.

title: FraudBench: Stress-Testing Policy-Grounded Banking Agents Against Adaptive Fraud
summary: Conversational agents now act for end users through tools while holding access to customer databases and internal policy documents that a caller can reach through dialogue alone. Banking is the clearest case: the same agent that answers a question can also change contact details, reset a PIN, or move money, so ordinary customer service is inseparable from authorization, fraud detection, and policy compliance. Existing financial-fraud benchmarks classify static transactions or messages, and general agent-safety benchmarks target prompt injection or generic harmful use; none test whether a policy-grounded banking agent safely acts when a caller manipulates identity, authorization, and trust over a conversation. We introduce FraudBench, an executable benchmark built on the $τ^2$-bench dual-control framework and the $τ$-Knowledge banking environment. Both the agent and the simulated caller act through tools over shared, mutable account state, and the agent may grant the caller access to selected tools; the environment exposes a 698-document internal policy corpus that the agent must retrieve from. FraudBench contains 150 authored adversarial scenarios; a frozen public set of 107 (90 across ten fraud mechanisms plus 17 chained adaptive attacks) is used for all reported runs, with 43 further chained attacks held out. Safety is history-dependent: single-control tasks satisfy every precondition but one, and adaptive attacks make a later, locally valid request unsafe because of an earlier probe, admission, or failed attempt. Each scenario is annotated with observable evidence, prohibited actions, safe dispositions, and intervention points. A preliminary single-trial evaluation of four agents on the 107 graded tasks yields attack-security between 49\% and 65\%, with money-mule and first-party fraud the most common cross-model weaknesses.

AI.tldr: FraudBench: A conversational benchmark testing banking agents' vulnerability to fraud through identity manipulation and policy compliance failures in dynamic dialogues.
AI.motivation: Current fraud benchmarks only classify static transactions or messages, while general agent-safety benchmarks focus on prompt injection or generic harmful use. There's a gap in testing whether policy-grounded banking agents can safely handle conversational fraud where callers manipulate identity, authorization, and trust over extended dialogues.
AI.method: Developed FraudBench using the τ²-bench dual-control framework and τ-Knowledge banking environment. Both agent and simulated caller act through tools over shared mutable account state, with the agent potentially granting caller access to selected tools. Includes 150 adversarial scenarios (107 public benchmark tasks) where safety is history-dependent, with single-control tasks and adaptive chained attacks.
AI.result: Preliminary evaluation of four agents on 107 graded tasks shows attack-security between 49% and 65%. Money-mule and first-party fraud were the most common cross-model weaknesses.
AI.conclusion: FraudBench addresses critical safety gaps in conversational banking agents by testing their vulnerability to sophisticated fraud schemes involving identity manipulation and policy compliance failures, revealing significant security vulnerabilities in current implementations.

title: SingularClip: Preventing Spectral Collapse to Maintain Plasticity in Continual and Reinforcement Learning
summary: Neural networks trained on nonstationary tasks frequently lose the ability to fit new targets, a phenomenon referred to as loss of plasticity. We identify a novel source of plasticity loss due to the growing anisotropy of weight matrices' singular values during training, and analyze this phenomenon both empirically and theoretically. To mitigate this issue, we introduce SingularClip, a procedure that periodically clips the singular values of all weight matrices. We show that SingularClip performs strongly against baselines across a range of tasks in both continual supervised learning and deep reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: SingularClip: A method to prevent loss of plasticity in neural networks by clipping singular values to maintain weight matrix isotropy during training on nonstationary tasks.
AI.motivation: Neural networks trained on nonstationary tasks often experience loss of plasticity - they lose the ability to fit new targets. The paper identifies that this is caused by growing anisotropy (uneven distribution) of weight matrices' singular values during training.
AI.method: Introduces SingularClip, a procedure that periodically clips the singular values of all weight matrices to maintain their isotropy and prevent excessive anisotropy that causes plasticity loss.
AI.result: SingularClip outperforms baselines across various tasks in both continual supervised learning and deep reinforcement learning settings, effectively mitigating plasticity loss.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropy in weight matrices' singular values is a key factor in plasticity loss, and SingularClip provides an effective solution by maintaining matrix isotropy, enabling neural networks to retain plasticity during training on nonstationary tasks.

title: Efficient Adaptation of LLMs for Hate Speech Detection in Low-Resource Languages: A Comparative Study on Roman Urdu
summary: It is challenging to detect hate speech in Low Resource Languages (LRLs) because of the absence of annotated data, the informality of its language structure, and the lack of standardized grammar. A good example of such a challenge is Roman Urdu which is broadly used by South Asians on social media and has a high variation while lacking contextually consistent spellings. The objective of this paper is to conduct a comprehensive assessment of Large Language Models (LLMs) for Hate Speech Detection (HSD) in Roman Urdu script and fine-tune these models using the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method called Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). To evaluate zero-shot inference, we benchmarked it against PEFT on different transformer models, including Mistral, LLaMA, Falcon, and multilingual BERT. Experiments are conducted on the PURUTT (Parallel Urdu and Roman Urdu Corpus for Toxic Comments and Transliteration) dataset with over 72,000 annotated comments. The results suggest that zero shot models perform moderately (F1 = 0.56), but updating a small fraction of the model trainable parameters improves the classification performance significantly (F1 > 0.93). Our results have shown that PEFT delivers outstanding performance alongside excellent computational efficiency, making it highly suitable for low-resource language processing tasks.

AI.tldr: LLMs with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT/LoRA) achieve superior hate speech detection in Roman Urdu (F1>0.93) compared to zero-shot approaches (F1=0.56), demonstrating effective solutions for low-resource languages with limited annotated data.
AI.motivation: Hate speech detection in Low Resource Languages (LRLs) like Roman Urdu is challenging due to lack of annotated data, informal language structure, inconsistent spellings, and absence of standardized grammar, despite its widespread use on South Asian social media.
AI.method: Comprehensive assessment of LLMs for Roman Urdu hate speech detection using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Evaluated zero-shot inference against PEFT on transformer models (Mistral, LLaMA, Falcon, multilingual BERT) using the 72,000+ annotated PURUTT dataset.
AI.result: Zero-shot models perform moderately (F1 = 0.56), but PEFT with minimal parameter updates significantly improves classification performance (F1 > 0.93). PEFT delivers outstanding performance with excellent computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: PEFT/LoRA is highly suitable for low-resource language processing tasks, providing both superior hate speech detection performance and computational efficiency, addressing key challenges in Roman Urdu and similar LRL contexts.

title: When Does Dynamic Ensembling Pay Off? Diagnosing Regionwise Gains in Regression under Distribution Shift
summary: Whether input-dependent ("dynamic") combination of a regression model pool beats the best static blend depends on the shift and is rarely known before deployment. Can a small labeled target-domain probe tell us when reallocating trust across regions of the input space will pay off? We answer this with $\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{CF5}}$, which estimates from the probe the cross-fitted gain of the regionwise convex combination over the best static convex blend: the realizable value of deciding, region by region, whom to trust. Across a frozen suite of 12 dataset-shift pairs (spatial, temporal, domain, feature-cluster), $\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{CF5}}$ predicts realized regionwise test gains with dataset-level Spearman $+0.98$ (95% CI $[+0.83, +1.00]$; $p=5\times10^{-5}$), including two cases overturning preregistered expectations. The relationship holds in a 16-pair sensitivity analysis (Spearman $+0.83$), whereas alternative probe diagnostics reach at most $+0.66$. This contrast isolates regional trust reallocation: correlation is $+0.98$ for regionwise-convex gain, but $+0.01$ for smooth covariate-dependent stacking after affine correction. A controlled generator shows dynamic gains arise from the interaction of shift heterogeneity and local competence, increase with shift severity, and become realizable between 128 and 256 probe labels in the tested grid. The Probe-Validated Ensemble Selector chooses among a static affine stacker and dynamic realizers, deploying a candidate only when a held-out lower confidence bound clears the static-convex floor. In a preregistered prospective batch, it matched or improved the floor in all 12 runs; two deployments reduced test risk by 11% and 16%, while the gate rejected a candidate whose un-gated deployment incurred $>30\times$ the static loss. We release OpenRegShift, a reproducible evaluation harness for regression ensembles under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: A method called $\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{CF5}}$ estimates from a small labeled probe whether dynamic, region-wise trust reallocation across regression models beats the best static blend under distribution shift, enabling validated ensemble selection.
AI.motivation: Whether dynamic combination of regression models beats static blends depends on distribution shifts that are rarely known before deployment. Current methods lack ways to predict from small target-domain probes when region-wise trust reallocation will pay off.
AI.method: Proposed $\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{CF5}}$ estimator that measures cross-fitted gain of regionwise convex combinations over best static convex blend from small labeled probes. Includes Probe-Validated Ensemble Selector with held-out confidence bounds and OpenRegShift evaluation framework.
AI.result: $\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{CF5}}$ predicts regionwise test gains with Spearman +0.98 across 12 dataset-shift pairs. In preregistered prospective batch, matched/improved static floor in all 12 runs, with two deployments reducing test risk by 11% and 16%, while preventing a harmful deployment.
AI.conclusion: Small labeled probes can reliably indicate when dynamic, region-wise trust reallocation is beneficial under distribution shift, enabling safe ensemble selection through validated decision rules that prevent harmful deployments.

title: RDFdL: Integrating RDF with Differential Dynamic Logic
summary: Knowledge graphs modeled in RDF are powerful for describing static knowledge, but they cannot capture or reason about the dynamic behavior of physical systems, e.g., systems described by differential equations, which is a critical gap for AI-driven cyber-physical systems. To solve this, we propose RDFdL, a framework that integrates RDF with Differential Dynamic Logic (dL) to represent and reason about both static knowledge and the continuous dynamics of physical systems. For the dynamic part, we syntactically represent differential equations and ranges in the state space in RDF and SHACL and provide semantics using a translation to dL. Linking RDF and dL through their shared foundation in first-order logic achieves a unique integration: verification results for safety and reachability properties in the dynamic logic domain become available as entailment to SPARQL queries over RDF data. We implement the pipeline using Apache Jena for ontology-driven RDF reasoning and KeYmaera X, the theorem prover for dL, and sketch its applicability in manufacturing.

AI.tldr: RDFdL integrates RDF knowledge graphs with Differential Dynamic Logic (dL) to represent and reason about both static knowledge and continuous physical system dynamics, enabling safety verification results to become SPARQL query entailments.
AI.motivation: RDF knowledge graphs effectively describe static knowledge but cannot capture or reason about dynamic physical system behavior described by differential equations, creating a critical gap for AI-driven cyber-physical systems.
AI.method: Propose RDFdL framework that integrates RDF with dL using their shared foundation in first-order logic, syntactically representing differential equations and state space ranges in RDF/SHACL, providing semantics via translation to dL, and implementing pipeline with Apache Jena and KeYmaera X theorem prover.
AI.result: Achieves unique integration where verification results for safety and reachability properties in the dynamic logic domain become available as entailment to SPARQL queries over RDF data, demonstrating applicability in manufacturing scenarios.
AI.conclusion: RDFdL bridges the gap between static knowledge representation and dynamic physical system reasoning, enabling comprehensive AI-driven analysis of cyber-physical systems through combined use of RDF knowledge graphs and differential dynamic logic verification.

title: Selection, Recombination, or a Fresh Solve? A Candidate-Free Control for Single-Pass Test-Time Aggregation
comment: Accepted at the COLM 2026 Workshop on Efficient Reasoning. 18 pages
summary: When every candidate is wrong, correct-candidate selection is unavailable, yet the aggregation call can still solve the problem afresh. A correct aggregate answer may therefore reflect recombination, fresh solving, or both. For efficient test-time reasoning, the relevant question is whether candidate context adds value beyond the additional generation pass. We introduce the missing candidate-free control under the same maximum output-token allowance and stratify by the number of correct candidates. Across AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025 with Qwen3-4B, candidate conditioning improves accuracy when multiple candidates are correct ($Δ_{\mathrm{cand}}$(c2+) = +0.290), lowers accuracy when every candidate is wrong ($Δ_{\mathrm{cand}}$(c0) = -0.123), and remains unresolved in the one-correct regime. The c2+ and c0 conclusions survive a conservative correction for the adaptive two-benchmark procedure. Under this counterfactual, the interpretation of all-wrong recovery reverses at this scale: conditioning on an all-wrong candidate pool lowers accuracy relative to a fresh solve. Original-format matching and placebo results characterize the failures descriptively but leave their mechanism unresolved. Within a separate structured intervention, explicit answer fields causally steer outputs toward their values; masking yields no measurable accuracy improvement, and equivalence with the original format was not established. The evidence is limited to one Qwen3-4B family, two mathematics benchmarks, first-answer-truncated candidate fragments, and single-pass prompted aggregation.

AI.tldr: Candidate aggregation in reasoning improves accuracy when multiple candidates are correct but harms accuracy when all candidates are wrong, with fresh solving sometimes outperforming aggregating over incorrect candidates.
AI.motivation: When all candidate solutions to a problem are wrong, correct selection becomes impossible, but aggregation could potentially solve the problem fresh. The key question is whether conditioning on candidate solutions adds value beyond simply generating a fresh solution, which is important for efficient test-time reasoning.
AI.method: Introduced a missing candidate-free control under the same maximum output-token allowance. Used stratified analysis by number of correct candidates. Tested on AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025 with Qwen3-4B model. Used original-format matching and placebo results to characterize failures. Conducted separate structured interventions with explicit answer fields to causally steer outputs.
AI.result: Candidate conditioning improves accuracy when multiple candidates are correct (Δ_cand(c2+) = +0.290), lowers accuracy when every candidate is wrong (Δ_cand(c0) = -0.123), and remains unresolved with one correct candidate. The c2+ and c0 conclusions survive conservative correction for adaptive two-benchmark procedure. Fresh solving outperforms conditioning on all-wrong candidate pools at this scale. Structured interventions show explicit answer fields causally steer outputs, but masking yields no measurable accuracy improvement.
AI.conclusion: Candidate aggregation is beneficial when multiple candidates are correct but detrimental when all candidates are wrong, suggesting fresh solving may be better than aggregating over incorrect solutions. However, evidence is limited to one model family, two math benchmarks, specific candidate fragments, and single-pass aggregation.

title: Adversarial Review: Structured Disagreement for Grounded Agentic Code Review
comment: Accepted to ICML 2026 Workshop on DL4C
summary: Early multi-agent LLM systems often used role-separated teams, yet scaling agent count yields diminishing returns on repository-level coding tasks. Recent alternatives treat agents as passive tools (subagents), yet this removes the benefits of agent interaction entirely. We study whether a subagent paradigm can support a middle ground: minimal agentic cooperation without the overhead of large multi-agent teams. We introduce Adversarial Review (AR), a minimal cooperative code-review protocol in which a main coding agent works with a reviewer and a critic agent. The reviewer evaluates code, while the critic audits the review through structured disagreement before the main agent edits. On LiveCodeBench, AR achieves the highest pass rate among tested methods, outperforming a five-agent baseline while using only three agents. On SWE-PRBench, naive AR exposes a false-consensus failure mode, where agents converge on agreement without sufficient evidence, but a single prompt iteration that adds disagreement explicitly achieves the highest F1 among tested methods. On SWE-bench Verified, AR also shows improvements over the baselines on repository-level coding tasks. Together, AR demonstrates that cooperative code review does not require many agents or complex communication structures: it requires that disagreement be minimal, structured, and evidence-grounded.

AI.tldr: Adversarial Review (AR) introduces a minimal 3-agent cooperative code-review protocol (coder, reviewer, critic) that achieves state-of-the-art performance on coding benchmarks through structured disagreement, showing that effective cooperation doesn't require large multi-agent teams.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the limitations of current multi-agent LLM systems for coding tasks: large role-separated teams show diminishing returns, while treating agents as passive tools removes benefits of agent interaction. The authors seek a middle ground that enables minimal agentic cooperation without the overhead of large teams.
AI.method: Adversarial Review (AR), a 3-agent protocol: 1) main coding agent writes code, 2) reviewer evaluates the code, 3) critic audits the review through structured disagreement before the main agent makes edits. This creates minimal, structured, evidence-grounded disagreement rather than false consensus.
AI.result: On LiveCodeBench, AR achieves highest pass rate among tested methods, outperforming 5-agent baseline with only 3 agents. On SWE-PRBench, naive AR shows false-consensus issues, but adding explicit disagreement achieves highest F1. On SWE-bench Verified, AR shows improvements over baselines for repository-level coding tasks.
AI.conclusion: Effective cooperative code review doesn't require many agents or complex communication structures. The key is having disagreement that is minimal, structured, and evidence-grounded. AR demonstrates this principle through its simple 3-agent protocol that outperforms larger teams.

title: Vector Symbolic Policy Gradient
summary: We answer this question with Vector-Symbolic Policy Gradient (VSPG), a discrete-action actor that represents each action by a unit-norm hypervector and scores it by similarity to the encoded state. Under the standard softmax policy-gradient surrogate, we prove that its update is exactly advantage-weighted hypervector bundling followed by normalization, and therefore supports standard advantage estimators. We further show that each trained action hypervector is a fixed-size compressed kernel memory, storing an advantage-weighted kernel expansion over visited states and transferring evidence according to the encoder-induced similarity. This provides a concrete mechanism that can support sample-efficient learning without increasing inference-time memory. Finally, for bipolar action memories, we prove that greedy action selection is stable under random bit flips, with failure probability decaying exponentially in the hypervector dimension. VSPG thus connects VSA action memories, log-linear policy gradients, and kernel policy search while providing a quantitative robustness guarantee.

AI.tldr: VSPG is a discrete-action actor that uses hypervectors to represent actions, connects vector symbolic architectures with policy gradients, provides kernel memory interpretation, and offers robustness guarantees against bit flips.
AI.motivation: To bridge vector symbolic architectures (VSA) with reinforcement learning policy gradients, enabling discrete-action learning with hypervector representations that offer compact memory storage, sample efficiency, and robustness guarantees.
AI.method: Vector-Symbolic Policy Gradient (VSPG) represents each discrete action as a unit-norm hypervector and scores actions by their similarity to an encoded state. Uses softmax policy-gradient surrogate, which results in advantage-weighted hypervector bundling followed by normalization. Each trained action hypervector becomes a compressed kernel memory storing advantage-weighted kernel expansions.
AI.result: Proves that VSPG's update is exactly advantage-weighted hypervector bundling with normalization, shows trained action hypervectors are fixed-size compressed kernel memories, demonstrates evidence transfer via encoder-induced similarity, and proves greedy action selection is stable under random bit flips with exponentially decaying failure probability in hypervector dimension.
AI.conclusion: VSPG successfully connects VSA action memories, log-linear policy gradients, and kernel policy search while providing quantitative robustness guarantees and enabling sample-efficient learning without increasing inference-time memory requirements.

title: Looped Language Models Improve Compositional Tool Calling
summary: Looped language models have shown promising results on reasoning benchmarks, yet their potential for agentic tool use remains largely unexplored. We study this question in compositional tool-calling settings, where models must coordinate multiple API calls, maintain intermediate state, and preserve dependencies across tool interactions. We evaluate native and retrofitted looped language models on API-Bank, BFCL, and NESTful, comparing looped and non-looped models trained under matched supervised fine-tuning recipes and varying recurrent depth at inference time. In controlled experiments, recurrent computation generally benefits compositional and dependency-aware tool use, while providing smaller and more model-dependent gains on isolated API invocation. Accuracy on multi-step tool use generally increases with recurrent depth; adaptive inference, however, achieves a more favorable compute-performance trade-off by allocating additional computation only when needed. Our results suggest that looped language models are a promising architecture for agentic systems that require reliable planning, coordination, and execution of compositional tool use workflows.

AI.tldr: Looped language models improve compositional tool-calling performance through recurrent computation, with adaptive inference providing optimal compute-performance trade-offs for agentic systems.
AI.motivation: While looped language models have shown promise on reasoning benchmarks, their potential for agentic tool use remains unexplored, particularly in compositional settings requiring coordination of multiple API calls, state maintenance, and dependency preservation.
AI.method: Evaluated native and retrofitted looped language models on API-Bank, BFCL, and NESTful benchmarks, comparing looped vs. non-looped models trained under matched supervised fine-tuning recipes with varying recurrent depth at inference time.
AI.result: Recurrent computation benefits compositional and dependency-aware tool use, with accuracy generally increasing with recurrent depth; adaptive inference achieves better compute-performance trade-off by allocating additional computation only when needed.
AI.conclusion: Looped language models are a promising architecture for agentic systems requiring reliable planning, coordination, and execution of compositional tool use workflows.

title: Role-Conditioned Sub-Token Routing for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models process long multimodal token sequences, making inference expensive in both memory and computation. Existing efficiency methods mainly reduce visual tokens, but aggressive token pruning becomes fragile because removing a token discards its entire representation. Sub-token compression provides a complementary alternative by retaining more tokens while reducing their value width. However, directly applying sub-token compression to VLA policies is less effective because information important for perception, language understanding, and control is distributed differently across the multimodal representation.
  We introduce Role-Conditioned Sub-Token Routing (RoleSub), which learns how to compress the value representations of retained tokens. After visual token reduction, RoleSub partitions each retained value representation into groups in an orthogonal space and uses a lightweight router to determine which groups should be preserved. The routing decision is conditioned on the token representation, a learned latent role representation, and language context. The same mechanism can also be applied to language values, allowing visual and language representations to be compressed without removing additional tokens.
  We evaluate RoleSub on OpenVLA-OFT-7B across the four LIBERO suites. At matched visual-KV budgets, RoleSub outperforms a trained token-only control in 33 of 36 settings, with the largest gains under aggressive compression. Combining visual and language compression reduces total KV to 9.2--11.3% of the original while retaining strong control performance on most tasks. These results show that reducing the representation within retained tokens provides an effective complement to token pruning for aggressive VLA compression.

AI.tldr: RoleSub is a sub-token compression method for VLA models that conditionally routes value representation groups based on token roles and language context, enabling more efficient multimodal inference while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: VLA models are computationally expensive due to long multimodal token sequences. Existing token pruning methods discard entire representations, becoming fragile under aggressive compression. Sub-token compression offers an alternative but current approaches are ineffective for VLA policies due to uneven distribution of important information across multimodal representations.
AI.method: Role-Conditioned Sub-Token Routing (RoleSub) compresses value representations of retained tokens by partitioning them into groups in orthogonal space and using a lightweight router to determine which groups to preserve. Routing decisions are conditioned on token representations, learned latent roles, and language context. The method can be applied to both visual and language values.
AI.result: RoleSub outperforms token-only compression in 33 out of 36 settings on OpenVLA-OFT-7B across LIBERO suites, with largest gains under aggressive compression. Combined visual and language compression reduces total KV to 9.2-11.3% of original while maintaining strong control performance on most tasks.
AI.conclusion: Sub-token compression effectively complements token pruning for VLA models, enabling aggressive compression while preserving performance through role-conditioned routing that respects the different information distribution across multimodal representations.

title: On the Triangle Inequality for the Jaccard Distance in Arbitrary Lattices
summary: This paper presents new theoretical results on generalizing the Jaccard distance for lattices and real valuations. We demonstrate that when the valuation is strictly positive, monotone, and modular, the Jaccard distance satisfies the triangle inequality on arbitrary lattices, effectively generalizing earlier results that depended heavily on distributivity. Moving to relatively complemented distributive lattices (which safely drop the requirement for the global bounds found in Boolean algebras), we prove the triangle inequality holds as long as the valuation is positive, monotone, supermodular, and $\log$-submodular. Additionally, we adapt the symmetric-difference Jaccard formulation for submodular valuations to sectionally complemented distributive lattices. Shifting to necessary conditions, we prove that supermodularity is a strict requirement for the standard generalized Jaccard distance to operate as a valid metric. Finally, we map the practical value of relaxing these structural constraints to computational fields like quantum information theory, formal concept analysis, and machine learning, closing with a brief look at open mathematical problems.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Jaccard distance theory from Boolean algebras to broader lattice classes with modular/supermodular valuations, proving triangle inequality conditions and exploring computational applications.
AI.motivation: To generalize Jaccard distance beyond Boolean algebras and distributive lattices, expanding its applicability to various lattice structures while identifying necessary conditions for metric validity.
AI.method: Mathematical analysis using lattice theory properties: 1) For arbitrary lattices with strictly positive, monotone, modular valuations; 2) For relatively complemented distributive lattices with positive, monotone, supermodular, log-submodular valuations; 3) Adaptation for submodular valuations in sectionally complemented distributive lattices; 4) Proof of supermodularity as necessary condition.
AI.result: 1) Jaccard distance satisfies triangle inequality on arbitrary lattices with strict modular valuations; 2) Triangle inequality holds for relatively complemented distributive lattices with supermodular/log-submodular valuations; 3) Successful adaptation for submodular valuations in specific distributive lattices; 4) Proved supermodularity is necessary for standard generalized Jaccard distance to be a metric.
AI.conclusion: The work successfully generalizes Jaccard distance theory across various lattice classes with specific valuation properties, demonstrates practical applications in computational fields, and identifies open mathematical problems for future research.

title: The Road Taken: The Role of Optimizers at the Edge of Stability
summary: The edge of stability refers to a phenomenon in deep learning with gradient-based optimizers where the Hessian eigenvalues of the loss remain stable above a threshold that the classical descent lemma predicts to be unstable. Previous works formulate the edge of stability with respect to the maximum Hessian eigenvalue and the learning rate. However, we observe that many first-order methods, including gradient descent, significantly violate the stability bound predicted by these theories by a factor as large as $\times 21.1$. Moreover, this deviation turns out to be systematic and highly dependent on the underlying optimizer, which is not captured by previous formulations. This calls for a new formulation of the stability threshold, which we derive from the directional Hessian and the gradient-alignment score with respect to the actual update taken by the optimizer, rather than the maximum curvature mode. Our new formulation of the realized edge of stability not only removes optimizer-dependent offsets and provides more consistent predictions of the stability threshold, but also introduces new diagnostic tools that reveal the unique role of the optimizer in actively balancing between the temporal and spatial budgets in first-order optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new formulation for the "edge of stability" phenomenon that accounts for optimizer-dependent deviations from classical stability predictions by using directional Hessian and gradient-alignment scores.
AI.motivation: Previous theories about the edge of stability focus on maximum Hessian eigenvalues and learning rates, but observations show that first-order methods (including gradient descent) systematically violate these stability bounds by large factors (up to ×21.1), and this deviation depends significantly on the optimizer used. This discrepancy calls for a reformulation of stability thresholds.
AI.method: The authors derive a new formulation of the stability threshold based on the directional Hessian and gradient-alignment score with respect to the actual update taken by the optimizer, rather than focusing on maximum curvature modes. This creates a "realized edge of stability" concept.
AI.result: The new formulation removes optimizer-dependent offsets and provides more consistent predictions of stability thresholds. It also introduces diagnostic tools that reveal how optimizers actively balance between temporal and spatial budgets in first-order optimization.
AI.conclusion: Classical stability analysis focusing on maximum Hessian eigenvalues is insufficient; a directional approach accounting for actual optimizer updates provides more accurate predictions and reveals the optimizer's active role in balancing optimization trade-offs.

title: GenEx: A Graph-Based Representational Paradigm for SARS-CoV-2 Variant Detection via Codon Co-occurrence Networks
summary: Genomic analysis on viruses such as SARS-CoV-2 variants: Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Omicron is heavily dominated by classical bioinformatics methods, including Sequence Alignment, Phylogenetic Analysis, and Mutation Frequency Statistics. These approaches use pairwise codon or nucleotide distance matrices to analyze gene sequences, treating them as linear strings rather than capturing their complex contextual interdependencies. We proposed GenEx, a pipeline that converts raw gene sequences into codon co-occurrence graphs and extracts more than 25 graph features. Our two most prominent techniques for graph generation and feature extraction are MSCG (Multi-Scale Codon Co-occurrence Graph) and LAPCG (Linear-time Adjacency PMI Codon Graph). Using these algorithms, we treated codon sequences as structured symbolic vocabularies interpretable to codon co-occurrence graph analysis, a representational paradigm borrowed from computational linguistics. Another major contribution includes implementing a spectral graph feature extraction using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), using the squared singular value ($σ^2$) instead of the traditionally used eigenvalue, which helped us to amplify the separation between dominant and subdominant spectral components, thereby enhancing inter-class separability in downstream classification. And to further demonstrate that our method works, we trained 23 benchmarked ML models against the latest SARS-CoV-2 variants, achieving remarkable results in detecting all SARS-CoV-2 variants.

AI.tldr: GenEx converts viral gene sequences into codon co-occurrence graphs using linguistic-inspired representations (MSCG/LAPCG) with spectral feature extraction via SVD using σ², achieving strong classification of SARS-CoV-2 variants.
AI.motivation: Current genomic analysis of viruses like SARS-CoV-2 variants relies heavily on classical bioinformatics methods (sequence alignment, phylogenetic analysis, mutation frequency statistics) that treat gene sequences as linear strings, failing to capture complex contextual interdependencies between codons.
AI.method: Proposed GenEx pipeline that converts raw gene sequences into codon co-occurrence graphs using two main techniques: MSCG (Multi-Scale Codon Co-occurrence Graph) and LAPCG (Linear-time Adjacency PMI Codon Graph). Applied computational linguistics principles to treat codon sequences as structured symbolic vocabularies. Implemented spectral graph feature extraction using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) with squared singular values (σ²) instead of traditional eigenvalues to enhance inter-class separability.
AI.result: Trained 23 benchmarked ML models against the latest SARS-CoV-2 variants (Beta, Gamma, Delta, Omicron) and achieved remarkable results in detecting all SARS-CoV-2 variants, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: The GenEx pipeline provides a novel graph-based approach to viral genomic analysis that captures complex codon interdependencies, outperforming traditional linear string-based methods and enabling better classification of SARS-CoV-2 variants through enhanced feature representation.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Structure-Aware Numerical Reasoning in LLaMA 3.1 8B
summary: Recent work has shown that large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong numerical sequence modeling capabilities and show promise in time-series prediction. While LLMs display in-context learning capabilities, the mechanisms with which they accomplish time-series prediction remain unclear. Specifically, whether they truly understand the underlying structure, which at a minimum requires reasoning over first differences in the sequence of numbers. To study this, we investigate Llama 3.1-8B from a mechanistic interpretability point of view. Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging field concerned with the reverse engineering of the algorithms learned by neural networks such as LLMs. To assess Llamas' numerical sequence modeling capabilities and to facilitate our mechanistic interpretability analysis, we create a sequence modeling task that cannot be solved without picking up structural cues. Specifically, we sample n random numbers and repeat them with an offset. We find that Llama displays strong performance on our tasks suggesting that it can pick up on the underlying structure. To understand the mechanisms that allow it to do so, we perform probing experiments and activation patching based counterfactual analysis. Probing reveals that the model computes and stores first differences in its internal representations without explicit supervision, indicating that it tracks structural information about the sequence. Activation patching reveals that Llama retrieves the relevant first-difference with a mechanism similar to an induction circuit and subsequently adds it to the current value. Notably, our work represents one of the first studies to identify this form of concept induction in LLMs.

AI.tldr: LLMs can perform numerical sequence prediction by learning structural patterns, specifically tracking first differences without explicit supervision, using induction-like circuits to add them to current values.
AI.motivation: While LLMs show promising numerical sequence modeling and time-series prediction capabilities, it's unclear if they truly understand underlying structures or just memorize patterns. The paper aims to investigate whether LLMs can reason over first differences in sequences, which is the minimum requirement for structural understanding.
AI.method: The researchers use mechanistic interpretability (reverse engineering neural network algorithms) on Llama 3.1-8B. They create a specific sequence modeling task where n random numbers are repeated with an offset, which requires structural understanding to solve. They then conduct probing experiments to examine internal representations and activation patching for counterfactual analysis.
AI.result: Llama demonstrates strong performance on the task, showing it can detect underlying structure. Probing reveals the model computes and stores first differences in its internal representations without explicit supervision. Activation patching shows the model retrieves relevant first-differences using induction-like circuits and adds them to current values.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can indeed perform concept induction for numerical sequences by tracking structural information (first differences) and using induction mechanisms similar to induction circuits. This represents one of the first demonstrations of such concept induction in LLMs, providing insights into how they achieve numerical reasoning.

title: Redakto - The Incognito Tab for LLMs
comment: Accepted at WIPE-OUT 2026, 2nd Workshop on Machine Unlearning and Privacy Preservation at ECML-PKDD
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are being increasingly used in everyday applications. A major challenge in the context of LLMs or Artificial Intelligence (AI) in general is to ensure privacy when using them, meaning that personally identifiable information (PII) is removed from any text that enters an LLM. These challenges have become more urgent with novel EU legislation. Uncertainty around LLM usage with respect to privacy concerns in EU countries can be a major blocker for the speed of innovation and transfer from research to applications. Here we present \textbf{Redakto}, a tool that can be used for anonymizing text prior to feeding it to an LLM or other downstream text processing. We provide state-of-the-art functionalities for both redaction of PII but also when used for pseudonymization. These functionalities are exposed such that they can easily be used by end-users, through the Redakto web application, and by developers and researchers, via REST APIs and model context protocol (MCP) hooks. The implementation is fully open source, requires modest compute resources, and can be readily deployed on local hardware. In contrast to prior work and in order to better assess the quality of the anonymized texts, we conduct extensive empirical evaluations on textual data from legal and medical domain with respect to both privacy and utility of the redacted texts. Our empirical results demonstrate that the texts anonymized with different redaction strategies achieve utility scores on par with the original texts, suggesting that anonymization with Redakto can be used for LLM tasks without substantial negative impact for the tasks we explored.

AI.tldr: Redakto is an open-source text anonymization tool for LLMs that removes PII with state-of-the-art redaction and pseudonymization capabilities, available via web app and APIs.
AI.motivation: Privacy concerns with LLM usage, especially under new EU legislation, create uncertainty that blocks innovation and research-to-application transfer, requiring tools to anonymize text before processing.
AI.method: Redakto provides advanced PII redaction and pseudonymization functionalities exposed through a web application for end-users and REST APIs/MCP hooks for developers/researchers. The implementation is open-source, resource-efficient, and deployable on local hardware.
AI.result: Extensive empirical evaluations on legal and medical text data show that anonymized texts achieve utility scores comparable to original texts, with different redaction strategies performing effectively for LLM tasks without substantial negative impact.
AI.conclusion: Redakto enables effective text anonymization for LLM applications while maintaining utility, addressing privacy concerns and regulatory compliance needs to facilitate innovation in AI applications.

title: Adaptive Multi-Agent Feature Selection for Personalized Fall Risk Prevention
comment: 38 pages, 10 figures, 12 tables. Accepted at Machine Learning for Healthcare (MLHC 2026)
summary: Falls among older adults represent a major public health challenge driven by complex, time-varying interactions across multiple risk domains. Effective fall risk factor identification requires learning from heterogeneous longitudinal data while accounting for sparse and delayed fall-related outcome events. However, existing approaches are largely static and fail to adaptively model evolving, individualized risk factors across modalities and time. We propose PAFIR, a Personalized and Adaptive Feature selection framework for fall risk Identification and pRevention, which formulates adaptive feature selection as a reinforcement learning problem over longitudinal multimodal health data. PAFIR jointly models structural dependencies among correlated assessment variables and temporal dynamics in wearable-derived physical activity data, and learns adaptive selection policies across repeated study visits using reward signals derived from sparse fall incidence outcomes. We apply PAFIR to data from the Physio fEedback Exercise pRogram (PEER) cluster-randomized trial. Experimental results demonstrate that PAFIR more effectively captures longitudinal and structural patterns of feature relevance than state-of-the-art baselines, and enables dynamic, subject-specific feature selection. By adapting selected features over time, PAFIR supports more timely and personalized fall prevention strategies.

AI.tldr: PAFIR is a reinforcement learning framework for adaptive, personalized feature selection from multimodal longitudinal health data to identify and prevent falls in older adults.
AI.motivation: Falls in older adults are a major public health problem with complex, time-varying risk factors. Existing approaches are static and fail to adaptively model evolving individual risk factors across different data modalities and time, especially given sparse and delayed fall outcomes.
AI.method: PAFIR formulates adaptive feature selection as a reinforcement learning problem over longitudinal multimodal health data. It jointly models structural dependencies among correlated assessment variables and temporal dynamics in wearable-derived physical activity data. The framework learns adaptive selection policies across repeated study visits using reward signals derived from sparse fall incidence outcomes.
AI.result: When applied to data from the Physio fEedback Exercise pRogram (PEER) trial, PAFIR more effectively captures longitudinal and structural patterns of feature relevance than state-of-the-art baselines. It enables dynamic, subject-specific feature selection and supports more timely and personalized fall prevention strategies.
AI.conclusion: PAFIR represents an advancement in fall risk assessment by providing adaptive, personalized feature selection that evolves with individual risk profiles over time, addressing limitations of static approaches and better accounting for the complex, multimodal nature of fall risk factors.

title: Cacheable by Design? Training Mixture-of-Experts Routers for Locality Against the Edge Memory-Bandwidth Wall: A Pre-Registered Negative Result with a Systems Measurement Study
comment: Pre-registered negative result plus a systems measurement study. Code, router-telemetry tool (llama-moe-trace), traces, data manifests, and the frozen pre-registration: https://github.com/Shriniwas410/cacheable-by-design
summary: Serving a 235B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model on a single 8 GB GPU is bottlenecked not by compute but by memory bandwidth: decode must stream each token's active experts from whichever tier holds them, and on consumer hardware most experts sit on an SSD far slower than RAM. We quantify this bandwidth wall on Qwen3-235B (Q4_K_M, 134 GB): measured decode is 0.44 tok/s warm, matching a bytes-per-token / bandwidth model, while a batching scheme that should amortize one disk sweep instead collapses at batch 32 from paging thrash. We build llama-moe-trace, a zero-surgery router-telemetry tool, and measure routing on Qwen3-30B: adjacent-token expert reuse is 2.0x chance, 95% of traffic uses 52.5% of experts, and an LRU cache of 13.4% of experts serves 66% of requests. We then ask whether cacheability is trainable: we pre-register training of 137M MoE language models with auxiliary locality and domain router losses, under joint criteria on cache-miss reduction and perplexity. The mechanism works (misses down up to 60%; a 99% static-pin hit rate) but every configuration fails the pre-registered <=1% perplexity gate -- miss reduction and quality are tightly coupled. Concurrent StickyMoE reports the same loss as near-free on single-domain sub-25M models; on multi-domain 137M we find the tax real. Our contribution is this pre-registered, stricter-criterion, multi-domain evaluation plus edge-serving measurements. A 340M rung shows the tax does not shrink with scale (it rises slightly). We further show training-free cache-aware rerouting stacks with trained locality -- together ~80% miss reduction at <=3.4% perplexity at both sizes, far cheaper than either alone -- while domain-primed prefetching does not help. All code, traces, and the pre-registration are released.

AI.tldr: This paper studies memory bandwidth bottlenecks when serving large MoE models on consumer hardware, analyzes routing patterns for cacheability, trains MoE models with auxiliary losses to improve locality, and finds trade-offs between cache miss reduction and model quality.
AI.motivation: Serving large 235B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts models on single 8GB GPUs faces memory bandwidth bottlenecks, as most experts sit on slow SSDs rather than RAM, causing significant decode latency (0.44 tok/s). The authors want to understand if expert routing patterns can be exploited for caching and whether cacheability can be trained into MoE models without sacrificing quality.
AI.method: 1) Built llama-moe-trace tool for zero-surgery router telemetry to analyze routing patterns; 2) Measured Qwen3-30B routing patterns and cacheability; 3) Pre-registered training of 137M MoE models with auxiliary locality and domain router losses; 4) Evaluated cache-aware rerouting strategies; 5) Tested training-free cache-aware rerouting that stacks with trained locality; 6) Evaluated at different scales (up to 340M parameters).
AI.result: Found adjacent-token expert reuse is 2.0x chance, 95% of traffic uses 52.5% of experts, and an LRU cache of 13.4% experts serves 66% of requests. Trained locality reduces cache misses by up to 60% with 99% static-pin hit rate, but all configurations fail the pre-registered ≤1% perplexity gate. Cache-aware rerouting + trained locality achieves ~80% miss reduction at ≤3.4% perplexity. Domain-primed prefetching doesn't help. The cache-quality tradeoff persists across scales.
AI.conclusion: Memory bandwidth severely limits MoE model serving on consumer hardware. While routing patterns show cacheability and training can improve locality, there's a fundamental trade-off between cache miss reduction and model quality that doesn't disappear with scale. The most effective approach combines trained locality with training-free cache-aware rerouting, but perfect cacheability without quality loss remains elusive.

title: Atrial Fibrillation Detection with Arbitrary Leads via a Codebook-Based Reconstruction-Classification Framework
summary: \textbf{Background and Objective}: Reliable atrial fibrillation (AF) detection from electrocardiogram (ECG) signals remains challenging in real-world clinical settings due to variable lead configurations, cross-dataset domain shifts, and pervasive physiological and technical artifacts. So we develop a robust and generalizable deep learning model for accurate AF detection.\\ \textbf{Methods}: We propose the Dual-Codebook Graph Collaborative Network (DCGCNet), a novel end-to-end vector-quantized variational autoencoder that jointly performs AF classification and ECG reconstruction. DCGCNet introduces two key components: (1) a Local-Global Contrastive Module for learning noise-invariant representations, and (2) an Adaptive Codebook Vector Quantizer that dynamically refines codebook prototypes to better align with input data distributions, thereby preventing codebook collapse and enhancing generalization.\\ \textbf{Results}: DCGCNet achieves state-of-the-art performance in standard intra-dataset 12-lead evaluation and demonstrates exceptional cross-dataset generalization across seven diverse settings, consistently attaining AUC > 0.98 in all cases. Furthermore, it maintains high diagnostic accuracy under realistic noisy conditions, including baseline wander, powerline interference, and EMG artifacts.\\ \textbf{Conclusions}: DCGCNet establishes a new benchmark for robust, generalizable, and noise-resilient AF detection, showing strong potential for deployment in real-world clinical environments.

AI.tldr: DCGCNet is a novel vector-quantized variational autoencoder that achieves state-of-the-art AF detection with exceptional cross-dataset generalization and noise resilience.
AI.motivation: AF detection from ECG signals is challenging in real-world settings due to variable lead configurations, cross-dataset domain shifts, and pervasive physiological/technical artifacts, necessitating robust and generalizable models.
AI.method: DCGCNet introduces a Dual-Codebook Graph Collaborative Network with two key components: (1) Local-Global Contrastive Module for noise-invariant representations, and (2) Adaptive Codebook Vector Quantizer that dynamically refines codebook prototypes to prevent collapse and enhance generalization.
AI.result: DCGCNet achieves state-of-the-art performance in intra-dataset 12-lead evaluation and exceptional cross-dataset generalization across seven diverse settings with AUC > 0.98 in all cases, maintaining high accuracy under realistic noisy conditions.
AI.conclusion: DCGCNet establishes a new benchmark for robust, generalizable, and noise-resilient AF detection, showing strong potential for real-world clinical deployment.

title: Evaluating Structured Information Extraction with Open Models in a High Risk Public Sector Application
comment: Accepted at Workshop on Systems Over Models: What Actually Works in Industry (SOMI-2026) at ECML 2026
summary: The extraction of structured information from unstructured documents represents a critical component of digital transformations in all sectors. While proprietary solutions dominate commercial applications, a rapidly growing ecosystem of open-source Optical Character Recognition (OCR) engines, Large Language Models (LLMs), and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) offers accessible alternatives. However, systematic evaluations on realistic, multi-step extraction pipelines remain scarce. Responsible usage of such extraction tools require comprehensive evaluations on realistic tasks, especially as these solutions will be key components of applications in the public sector that the EU AI act categorizes as high risk. To address this gap we present a comprehensive benchmark assessing the end-to-end performance of open-source systems on a complex real-world document processing task classified as high risk: Student applications for an international study program. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation with state-of-the-art OCR engines, LLMs and VLMs. Our results reveal that while VLMs generally outperform OCR+LLM pipelines, even state-of-the-art open-source models struggle to handle such tasks reliably in zero-shot settings.
