AI.motivation: Protein language models used for sequence design face a dilemma: guidance that's mild enough to preserve natural activation statistics barely changes properties, while strong guidance produces unnatural sequences that are hard to fold. Current methods fail to detect when guidance causes representational collapse.
AI.method: Introduce Mahalanobis filtering - a training-free post-hoc method that uses a cheap density prior over natural protein activations to detect off-manifold collapse. Sequences are filtered based on whether their activations remain statistically typical under this prior.
AI.result: Mahalanobis filtering improves both property scores and structural plausibility of sequences at negligible cost, without modifying the generator. It transfers across different guidance methods and exposes failures that property oracles alone cannot detect.
AI.conclusion: Off-manifold collapse is a detectable failure mode in protein language model guidance that can be cheaply identified and filtered post-hoc using activation statistics, providing a practical solution to the guidance strength dilemma.

title: FinRCA-Bench: Benchmarking Evidence Retrieval and Reasoning for Financial AI Systems
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/PratikGhawate/FinRCA-AI-Bench
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to support financial operations, but their apparent reasoning performance can depend on whether they receive the right evidence. In financial reconciliation, the evidence needed for diagnosis is distributed across invoices, purchase orders, approvals, allocations, payments, ledger entries, and bank activity, linked by transactional relationships rather than textual similarity. End-to-end accuracy can therefore conflate evidence access with reasoning quality. We introduce FinRCA-Bench, a deterministic synthetic benchmark of 2,250 accounts-payable-to-bank reconciliation cases spanning 14 operational tables, including 1,500 injected failures across 15 causal categories and 750 legitimate or hard-negative cases. Root-cause labels and record-level evidence contracts are hidden from the model, allowing retrieval to be evaluated independently of answer correctness. We compare Rules/SQL, classical machine learning, dense semantic retrieval, deterministic relational expansion, and Typed Provenance Graph Retrieval (TPGR), a typed traversal restricted to persisted transaction relationships. Rules/SQL reaches 84.97% held-out exact accuracy and classical ML reaches 95.44%. Holding the reasoning model, prompt, and generation settings fixed while changing only retrieval increases macro required-record recall from 0.83% to 77.70% and exact 16-class accuracy from 2.05% to 72.44%. Structural retrieval failures outnumber reasoning failures with sufficient retrieval by 95 to 15; 254 correct predictions occur despite incomplete retrieval, and strict returned-evidence contract accuracy is only 5.72%. On FinRCA-Bench, retrieval architecture strongly shapes observed AI-system performance, and a correct root-cause label is a weak proxy for an auditable diagnosis.

AI.tldr: FinRCA-Bench is a synthetic benchmark for evaluating financial reconciliation AI systems, showing that retrieval architecture dramatically affects observed performance and that correct answers don't guarantee auditable evidence.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of financial AI systems conflates evidence retrieval quality with reasoning performance, since financial evidence is distributed across multiple operational tables linked by transactional relationships rather than textual similarity.
AI.method: Created FinRCA-Bench with 2,250 accounts-payable-to-bank reconciliation cases across 14 operational tables, including 1,500 injected failures across 15 causal categories. Compared Rules/SQL, classical ML, dense semantic retrieval, deterministic relational expansion, and Typed Provenance Graph Retrieval (TPGR) - a typed traversal restricted to persisted transaction relationships.
AI.result: Retrieval architecture drastically impacts performance: changing only retrieval increased required-record recall from 0.83% to 77.70% and exact accuracy from 2.05% to 72.44%. Rules/SQL achieved 84.97% accuracy, classical ML 95.44%. Structural retrieval failures outnumbered reasoning failures 95 to 15 when retrieval was sufficient, and strict evidence contract accuracy was only 5.72%.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval architecture strongly shapes observed AI performance in financial reconciliation, and correct root-cause labels are weak proxies for auditable diagnoses, highlighting the need to evaluate retrieval and reasoning separately.

title: Denoising-Aware Inversion: Revealing Privacy Risks in Noise-Protected Text Embeddings
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted by IEEE ICDM 2026
summary: Dense text embeddings are widely used in data mining, retrieval, and downstream machine learning systems due to their compact and semantically rich representations, but recent embedding inversion attacks have shown that they can expose substantial information about the original text, leading to serious privacy leakage risks. A common defense is to release perturbed embeddings by adding Gaussian noise, which is simple yet effective against standard inversion attacks and does not significantly degrade embedding utility for downstream tasks. However, it remains unclear whether such noise-protected embeddings are sufficiently safe against adaptive attackers that explicitly account for the perturbation process. In this paper, we study text embedding inversion in a noise-protected setting, where the attacker can observe only noisy embeddings and has no access to clean embedding targets. We first analyze why existing generative inversion methods fail under this setting and identify a "Double Noise Trap", which fundamentally prevents standard generative inversion models from achieving high-quality reconstruction. To address this challenge, we propose DAEI, a denoising-aware embedding inversion pipeline that combines a residual denoising autoencoder with generative text inversion where the denoiser is trained in an unsupervised manner using Stein's unbiased risk estimate to enable denoising from noisy observations alone. Extensive experiments show that DAEI achieves approximately 154\% relative improvement in BLEU over the existing generative inversion baseline, while also improving token-level F1 and ROUGE-L by 32--60\%. The promising inversion performance of DAEI challenges the prevailing assumption that simple Gaussian perturbation is sufficient to prevent sensitive information leakage from embedding representations.

AI.tldr: DAEI (Denoising-Aware Embedding Inversion) successfully attacks noise-protected text embeddings by using a residual denoising autoencoder trained with Stein's unbiased risk estimate, achieving significant improvements over existing methods and challenging the assumption that Gaussian noise sufficiently protects embeddings from privacy leakage.
AI.motivation: Dense text embeddings are widely used but vulnerable to inversion attacks that expose private text information. While Gaussian noise perturbation is commonly used as a defense, it's unclear whether this protection holds against adaptive attackers who account for the perturbation process.
AI.method: Proposed DAEI: a denoising-aware embedding inversion pipeline combining a residual denoising autoencoder with generative text inversion. The denoiser is trained unsupervised using Stein's unbiased risk estimate to enable denoising from noisy embeddings alone, without access to clean targets.
AI.result: DAEI achieves approximately 154% relative improvement in BLEU over existing generative inversion baselines, with 32-60% improvements in token-level F1 and ROUGE-L. It successfully reconstructs text from noise-protected embeddings, demonstrating the vulnerability of current Gaussian perturbation defenses.
AI.conclusion: Simple Gaussian perturbation is insufficient to prevent sensitive information leakage from embedding representations, as DAEI's promising inversion performance challenges prevailing assumptions about embedding privacy protection.

title: Bridging Search and CRM: Productionizing AI Product Research Agents for Customer Re-Engagement
summary: Modern e-commerce platforms often operate search, recommendation, personalization, and CRM systems independently, limiting opportunities for proactive customer re-engagement. This is particularly challenging for exploratory intents such as best smartphones or latest 5G phones, where users may leave the platform for external research before purchasing. We present a scalable, production-deployed framework that bridges search and CRM workflows through AI-powered Product Research Agents. The system identifies users with exploratory purchase intent and low engagement, conducts grounded multi-agent product research using behavioral signals, external knowledge, and enterprise catalog data, and delivers personalized recommendations through WhatsApp. We evaluate the framework in a 23-day production deployment involving approximately 15K WhatsApp notifications for mobile product discovery. The campaign achieved substantial CTR improvements over traditional WhatsApp recommendation campaigns, with evidence of secondary engagement through message forwarding and sharing. The deployment also generated downstream purchases and GMV impact, demonstrating the practical effectiveness of AI Product Research Agents for proactive customer re-engagement and end-to-end customer journey optimization.

AI.tldr: AI-powered Product Research Agents bridge search and CRM workflows to proactively re-engage users with exploratory purchase intent through personalized WhatsApp recommendations, achieving improved CTR and downstream purchases.
AI.motivation: E-commerce platforms operate search, recommendation, personalization, and CRM systems independently, limiting proactive customer re-engagement opportunities, especially for users with exploratory purchase intent who may leave the platform for external research before buying.
AI.method: A scalable production-deployed framework using AI-powered Product Research Agents that: 1) identify users with exploratory purchase intent and low engagement, 2) conduct grounded multi-agent product research using behavioral signals, external knowledge, and enterprise catalog data, and 3) deliver personalized recommendations through WhatsApp.
AI.result: In a 23-day production deployment with ~15K WhatsApp notifications for mobile product discovery: achieved substantial CTR improvements over traditional WhatsApp campaigns, evidence of secondary engagement through message forwarding/sharing, and generated downstream purchases and GMV impact.
AI.conclusion: AI Product Research Agents are practically effective for proactive customer re-engagement and end-to-end customer journey optimization, bridging previously disconnected e-commerce systems to recapture users with exploratory purchase intent.

title: Scalable Geospatial Machine Learning for Power-Line Asset Risk: Integrating Remote Sensing for Lightning and Vegetation Risk Modelling
summary: Electric power networks are increasingly exposed to weather-sensitive failure mechanisms that require asset-level, spatially explicit risk modelling for effective intervention planning. This study contributes a modular, robust, and explainable probability-of-failure (PoF) modelling framework for utility asset management. The central contribution is an asset-level architecture that can be scaled to new environmental data sources and additional PoF types without reworking the underlying pipeline. This is particularly relevant for industry settings, where risk models must remain operationally maintainable while adapting to changing data availability, asset-management priorities, and climate-driven hazard conditions. We demonstrate the framework for vegetation-related and lightning-related failure modes using a harmonised geospatial machine-learning pipeline. The implementation integrates multi-source predictors, including topography (SRTM), vegetation condition (MODIS Normalised Difference Vegetation Index - NDVI), lightning climatology (LIS VHRMC), OpenStreetMap-derived proximity features, and utility operational records. The resulting architecture is computationally efficient, operationally extensible, and suitable for utility-scale deployment. It provides actionable asset-level risk stratification for inspection prioritisation, vegetation management, asset hardening, and resilience planning, supporting earlier intervention and more climate-resilient network operations.

AI.tldr: Developed a modular, scalable probability-of-failure framework for utility assets that integrates multiple environmental data sources for weather-related risk assessment, enabling asset-level prioritization for utility management.
AI.motivation: Electric power networks face increasing weather-related failures that require spatially explicit, asset-level risk modeling for effective intervention planning. Existing approaches need to be adaptable to changing data availability, asset management priorities, and climate conditions while remaining operationally maintainable.
AI.method: Developed a modular probability-of-failure modeling framework with asset-level architecture scalable to new environmental data sources and additional failure types. Implemented harmonized geospatial machine-learning pipeline integrating multi-source predictors: topography (SRTM), vegetation condition (MODIS NDVI), lightning climatology (LIS VHRMC), OpenStreetMap proximity features, and utility operational records.
AI.result: Created a computationally efficient and operationally extensible framework suitable for utility-scale deployment. Demonstrated the framework for vegetation-related and lightning-related failure modes, providing actionable asset-level risk stratification for inspection prioritization, vegetation management, asset hardening, and resilience planning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables earlier intervention and more climate-resilient network operations by providing a modular, robust, and explainable approach to asset-level risk modeling that can adapt to changing environmental conditions and data sources while supporting utility-scale decision-making.

title: FACET: Preserving Source Intent and Executable State in Terminal Task Synthesis
summary: Training terminal agents requires scalable executable supervision, yet synthesizing high-quality terminal tasks remains challenging. Each task couples an instruction, an initialized environment, a reference solution, and an executable verifier; if these artifacts are generated from inconsistent assumptions, the resulting task may be unsolvable or incorrectly evaluated. Meanwhile, multi-stage synthesis can discard the goals, dependencies, state transitions, and procedural constraints encoded in the original sources. We present FACET (Fine-grained Agentic Construction of Executable Tasks), a framework that addresses both information preservation and cross-artifact consistency. FACET reconstructs related agent skills into coherent, information-rich scenarios, then realizes and repairs the execution environment before generating the final task artifacts. The resulting container state serves as shared grounding for the instruction, solution, and verifier, while execution-based validation and targeted repair correct artifact-specific failures without unnecessarily regenerating valid components. FACET produces complex terminal tasks with dense executable checks, and successful trajectories collected from these tasks provide effective, data-efficient supervision. Fine-tuning models across multiple scales consistently improves performance on Terminal-Bench 2.1, while analyses of alternative generation schemes support the importance of environment-grounded construction for task validity and solution-verifier alignment. These results establish source-intent preservation and shared executable-state grounding as key principles for scalable terminal-task synthesis.

AI.tldr: FACET is a framework for synthesizing high-quality terminal tasks by preserving source intent information and ensuring cross-artifact consistency through environment-grounded construction and targeted repair.
AI.motivation: Current terminal task synthesis methods face challenges with inconsistent artifacts (instructions, environments, solutions, verifiers) that can create unsolvable tasks or incorrect evaluation. Multi-stage synthesis often discards important information from original sources like goals, dependencies, state transitions, and procedural constraints.
AI.method: FACET reconstructs related agent skills into coherent scenarios, realizes and repairs execution environments, and uses the resulting container state as shared grounding for generating consistent task artifacts. It employs execution-based validation and targeted repair to fix artifact-specific failures without regenerating valid components.
AI.result: FACET produces complex terminal tasks with dense executable checks. Training data collected from these tasks provides effective supervision. Fine-tuning models across multiple scales consistently improves performance on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Analysis shows environment-grounded construction is crucial for task validity and solution-verifier alignment.
AI.conclusion: Source-intent preservation and shared executable-state grounding are key principles for scalable terminal-task synthesis. FACET demonstrates that environment-grounded construction is essential for producing valid, consistent terminal tasks that provide effective supervision for training agents.

title: Coordination on a Budget: Federated Active Learning with Few Labels
summary:
Federated Active Learning (FAL) addresses the dual challenges of data privacy and label scarcity, where the absence of a global data view introduces additional hurdles for coordinated query selection. We study cross-silo FAL in the low-budget regime, where annotation decisions are most critical. We characterize, both theoretically and empirically, a heterogeneity reversal: in low-budget settings, homogeneous (IID) data requires stronger coordination to avoid redundant queries, whereas heterogeneous data naturally promotes diversity; this trend reverses at higher budgets. Thus, in contrast to the standard federated learning (FL) narrative where heterogeneity is a primary challenge, we show that IID settings are more challenging for query selection in FAL.
  Motivated by these findings, we propose a new FAL framework that utilizes federated representation learning to align client data in a shared embedding space. This enables the server to perform globally coordinated active selection over optionally obfuscated client embeddings, while annotation remains local to each client. Although our framework operates in the more challenging low-budget regime, it achieves performance that surpasses existing FAL methods even when they are given substantially larger annotation budgets, demonstrating the value of centralized coordination under privacy constraints.

AI.tldr: In low-budget Federated Active Learning (FAL), IID data requires stronger coordination to avoid redundant queries, while heterogeneous data naturally promotes diversity - a reversal of the standard FL narrative where heterogeneity is usually problematic.
AI.motivation: Federated Active Learning faces dual challenges of data privacy and label scarcity, with the absence of global data view making coordinated query selection difficult. The paper focuses on cross-silo FAL in low-budget regimes where annotation decisions are most critical.
AI.method: Proposes a new FAL framework using federated representation learning to align client data in a shared embedding space, enabling server-side globally coordinated active selection over optionally obfuscated client embeddings while keeping annotation local.
AI.result: Demonstrates heterogeneity reversal: in low-budget settings, IID data requires stronger coordination to avoid redundancy while heterogeneous data naturally promotes diversity (reversing at higher budgets). The proposed framework achieves performance surpassing existing FAL methods even with substantially larger annotation budgets.
AI.conclusion: Contrary to standard FL where heterogeneity is challenging, IID settings are more problematic for query selection in FAL. The proposed framework demonstrates the value of centralized coordination under privacy constraints, particularly effective in low-budget regimes.

title: Can a Lightweight Multimodal Model Estimate LLM Reasoning Performance? A Study for Compute-Optimal Document Inference
summary: Uniformly allocating inference reasoning budgets to LLMs is expensive and prone to over-thinking penalties; especially in document tasks where visual layouts drive complexity. To address this, we introduce BudgetDoc, the first multimodal benchmark providing explicit supervision for model-budget-performance trade-offs across three document tasks. Using BudgetDoc, we train DRB (Document-Reasoning Balancer), an approx. 1B-parameter pre-flight estimator (SigLIP-2 + Qwen3-0.6B) that predicts ordinal model performance across budget levels, achieving a 0.753 weighted F1. When dynamically allocating reasoning budgets across five frontier models and three datasets, DRB matches or improves F1 scores compared to always-maximum-budget baselines in 9 of 15 configurations while drastically reducing cost. Finally, preliminary evaluations demonstrate DRB's potential to generalize to cross-model selection.

AI.tldr: BudgetDoc is a multimodal benchmark for model-budget-performance trade-offs in document tasks, used to train DRB - a 1B-parameter estimator that dynamically allocates reasoning budgets to reduce costs while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Uniformly allocating maximum inference reasoning budgets to LLMs for document tasks is expensive and can lead to over-thinking penalties, especially since visual layouts in documents add complexity that may not require maximum computational resources.
AI.method: 1) Introduced BudgetDoc benchmark providing explicit supervision for model-budget-performance trade-offs across three document tasks. 2) Trained DRB (Document-Reasoning Balancer) - an approximately 1B-parameter pre-flight estimator combining SigLIP-2 and Qwen3-0.6B to predict ordinal model performance across budget levels. 3) Applied DRB to dynamically allocate reasoning budgets across five frontier models and three datasets.
AI.result: DRB achieved 0.753 weighted F1 score in performance prediction. In dynamic budget allocation experiments, DRB matched or improved F1 scores compared to always-maximum-budget baselines in 9 out of 15 configurations while drastically reducing computational costs. Preliminary evaluations show DRB's potential for cross-model selection generalization.
AI.conclusion: Budget allocation should be adaptive rather than uniform, and DRB demonstrates that intelligent budget allocation can maintain or improve performance while significantly reducing computational costs in document tasks, with potential for broader model selection applications.

title: ProxyGuard: Direct Reliability Inference for Randomized Data Release Mechanisms with Shared Targets
summary: Researchers often choose a proxy dataset from many releases, transformations, or seeds. Search can make an invalid release appear adequate, while one adequate release does not establish that its generator is reliable. ProxyGuard controls both errors using prespecified bounded risks and a sealed target set. Named-release mode corrects for multiplicity and certifies specific releases. Direct shared-target mode evaluates independent mechanism draws on a common target, lower-bounds their favorable-score rate, and subtracts a bound on favorable scores contributed by invalid releases. Conditional on the target, release scores are independent, yielding a finite-sample mechanism-reliability guarantee without independent target batches or assumptions on release-level $p$-value dependence. We show that the mean-only penalty is sharp and derive a smooth-score certificate with additive target concentration. In a registered three-requirement study, direct mode raises power from 5.6\% to 64.2\% at reliability 0.95, while named mode remains stronger under high-signal evidence. Prospective audits span full-pipeline Rice--TVAE, which retrains on every draw, and a non-tabular text mechanism.

AI.tldr: ProxyGuard provides statistical methods to certify the reliability of data generation mechanisms while controlling for false discoveries from multiple proxy dataset releases, offering two operational modes with finite-sample guarantees.
AI.motivation: Researchers often work with multiple releases, transformations, or seeds of proxy datasets. A key problem is that search across multiple releases can make invalid releases appear adequate, while finding one adequate release doesn't prove the reliability of the underlying data generation mechanism. There's a need for statistical methods that control both false discovery risks when evaluating multiple releases.
AI.method: ProxyGuard introduces two modes: (1) Named-release mode that corrects for multiplicity and certifies specific releases, and (2) Direct shared-target mode that evaluates independent mechanism draws on a common target set, lower-bounds their favorable-score rate, and subtracts a bound on favorable scores contributed by invalid releases. The method uses prespecified bounded risks and a sealed target set, requiring no independent target batches or assumptions on release-level p-value dependence.
AI.result: The paper shows that the mean-only penalty is sharp and derives a smooth-score certificate with additive target concentration. In a registered three-requirement study, the direct mode raises power from 5.6% to 64.2% at reliability 0.95, while named mode remains stronger under high-signal evidence. The methods were successfully applied to prospective audits including full-pipeline Rice-TVAE (which retrains on every draw) and a non-tabular text mechanism.
AI.conclusion: ProxyGuard provides practical statistical tools for establishing data generation mechanism reliability with formal error control, addressing the challenge of multiple releases in proxy dataset evaluation. The two complementary modes offer flexible solutions for different evidence scenarios, with strong empirical performance demonstrated in real-world applications.

title: CTIFoundry: An Agent-Native Corpus Scaffold for Cyber Threat Intelligence
summary: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) is increasingly consumed not by human analysts but by LLM agents that compose multi-step investigations at query time. The harness side of this shift has matured rapidly (planning loops, tool protocols, context management), but the corpus side has not: threat reports and vulnerability databases are still packaged for retrieval-augmented generation, as opaque chunks behind an embedding index. We argue that this substrate, not model capability, is the bottleneck on agentic CTI investigation, and present CTIFoundry, an agent-native corpus scaffold. At build time, CTIFoundry materializes the latent structure of a CTI corpus: a deterministic ontology graph over four authoritative knowledge bases (CVE, CWE, CAPEC, ATT&CK) whose official cross-references become typed, traversable edges; a span-grounded report layer whose canonical, alias-resolved cross-vendor entities index provenance-carrying chunks; and hybrid dense+lexical retrieval surfaces. At query time this structure is exposed through seven typed tools and three procedural skills mounted on a stock open-source agent harness. On the public CTIConnect benchmark, swapping only the action surface lifts the identically-harnessed agent by +0.19 to +0.28 overall F1 across a four-model, two-provider panel: a small model on CTIFoundry surpasses a flagship on the flat substrate, and the gain is not bought with search effort, since on both Claude models the scaffolded agent is more accurate at roughly half the tool calls. An ablation attributes it: typed structure carries the larger share, procedural skills convert structure into discipline, and the two compose super-additively, because skills bind only to structure that exists.

AI.tldr: CTIFoundry is an agent-native corpus scaffold that structures CTI data into a deterministic ontology graph and entity-grounded report layer, enabling better LLM agent investigations through typed tools and procedural skills.
AI.motivation: Current CTI corpus packaging for retrieval-augmented generation treats threat reports as opaque chunks behind embedding indexes, creating a bottleneck for LLM agent investigations despite advances in agent harness technology.
AI.method: CTIFoundry materializes latent structure from CTI corpus: 1) deterministic ontology graph from four knowledge bases (CVE, CWE, CAPEC, ATT&CK) with typed edges, 2) span-grounded report layer with canonical entities and provenance-carrying chunks, 3) hybrid dense+lexical retrieval surfaces. At query time, provides seven typed tools and three procedural skills on a standard agent harness.
AI.result: On CTIConnect benchmark, CTIFoundry improved agent performance by +0.19 to +0.28 overall F1 across four models/two providers. Small models with CTIFoundry surpassed flagship models on flat substrate. Claude models achieved higher accuracy with roughly half the tool calls. Ablation showed typed structure contributes most, procedural skills add discipline, and they compose super-additively.
AI.conclusion: The bottleneck in agentic CTI investigation is the corpus substrate, not model capability. CTIFoundry demonstrates that structured, agent-native corpora with typed tools and procedural skills significantly improve LLM agent performance in cyber threat intelligence investigations.

title: FlashAttention for Scalable Vector Architectures
summary: Inference with transformer models on CPUs is increasingly important, especially for Small Language Models (SLMs), where vector architectures are emerging as a promising execution substrate. The attention module is a major bottleneck due to high memory bandwidth requirements; FlashAttention mitigates this by fusing operations to improve data locality and reduce intermediate memory traffic. In this paper, we present FlashAttention-V, a blocked FlashAttention for scalable vector architectures that adapts efficiently from short to very long vectors by exploiting parallelism across attention heads, inter-head packing to enable efficient utilization of vector lengths beyond the head dimension, and improving vector register utilization and memory access locality. We integrate FlashAttention-V into ggml within llama.cpp and evaluate it on TinyLlama, Llama 3.2, Qwen2.5, and Pythia-410M using gem5 and a Banana Pi BPI-F3. On the Banana Pi BPI-F3, we confirm that loop reordering and loop unrolling across attention heads are effective optimization principles, scaling performance gains with larger models and most pronounced with short contexts and during decoding. Simulation-based analysis shows that FlashAttention-V achieves 22x-42x speedup over scalar FlashAttention at 512-bit VL in prefill, with an additional 2x-2.5x gain scaling to 64 lanes and 4096-bit VL. During decode, FlashAttention-V achieves 8x-11x speedup using 512-bit vector lengths over scalar FlashAttention, with performance showing diminishing sensitivity to vector width and lane count due to single-token, memory-bound execution. We further identify structural bottlenecks in Q8_0 quantized linear layers that limit arithmetic amortization under long-vector execution, consistent across RVV and Arm SVE, indicating that current quantization formats pose a fundamental challenge to long-vector scalability.

AI.tldr: FlashAttention-V: A vectorized FlashAttention for CPUs that exploits parallelism across attention heads and inter-head packing to scale efficiently with vector architectures, achieving up to 42x speedup over scalar implementations.
AI.motivation: Transformer inference on CPUs is important for SLMs, but attention modules suffer from high memory bandwidth requirements. While FlashAttention improves data locality, current implementations don't efficiently utilize vector architectures with varying vector lengths, especially for short contexts and decoding.
AI.method: FlashAttention-V adapts FlashAttention for scalable vector architectures through three key techniques: 1) parallelism across attention heads, 2) inter-head packing to efficiently use vector lengths beyond head dimension, and 3) improved vector register utilization and memory access locality. The approach is integrated into ggml within llama.cpp and evaluated on various models using gem5 simulations and Banana Pi BPI-F3 hardware.
AI.result: On Banana Pi BPI-F3, loop reordering and unrolling across attention heads scale with larger models, most effective with short contexts and decoding. FlashAttention-V achieves 22x-42x speedup over scalar FlashAttention at 512-bit VL in prefill, with 2x-2.5x additional gain scaling to 64 lanes and 4096-bit VL. During decode, achieves 8x-11x speedup with 512-bit vectors, though performance shows diminishing returns due to memory-bound execution. Also identifies bottlenecks in Q8_0 quantized linear layers that limit long-vector scalability.
AI.conclusion: FlashAttention-V demonstrates that blocked FlashAttention can effectively exploit vector architectures, achieving significant speedups for CPU-based transformer inference. However, current quantization formats pose fundamental challenges to long-vector scalability, suggesting need for quantization-aware vectorization approaches.

title: Preference Reasoning under Indeterminacy in Large Language Models
summary: As large language models evolve into decision-making agents, the ability to reason over preferences becomes fundamental to alignment, coordination, and collective intelligence. Yet, unlike standard benchmarks, real-world preference reasoning is inherently indeterminate: information may be incomplete, and valid solutions may not exist. We argue that indeterminacy, rather than correctness alone, is a central challenge for AI reasoning. We formalize this challenge along two axes, (i) epistemic indeterminacy, arising from incomplete, partial, or expressive preferences, and (ii) structural indeterminacy, arising from the non-existence of solutions under standard social choice concepts. Across a hierarchy of tasks, we show that state-of-the-art language models systematically fail to distinguish between determined and undetermined instances, exhibiting miscalibrated reasoning even in verification settings.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that indeterminacy in preference reasoning is a key challenge for AI agents, showing that current LLMs fail to distinguish between solvable and unsolvable preference problems.
AI.motivation: As LLMs evolve into decision-making agents, preference reasoning becomes crucial for alignment and coordination. Real-world preference reasoning is inherently indeterminate (incomplete information, potentially no valid solutions), making indeterminacy rather than just correctness a central AI reasoning challenge.
AI.method: The authors formalize indeterminacy along two axes: (1) epistemic indeterminacy from incomplete/partial preferences, and (2) structural indeterminacy from non-existent solutions under social choice concepts. They test state-of-the-art language models across a hierarchy of tasks.
AI.result: LLMs systematically fail to distinguish between determined and undetermined instances, exhibiting miscalibrated reasoning even in verification settings. They show poor performance in handling indeterminate preference reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Indeterminacy in preference reasoning is a fundamental challenge for AI agents that requires new approaches beyond standard correctness benchmarks. Current LLMs lack the ability to properly handle indeterminate scenarios, highlighting a critical gap for real-world AI decision-making.

title: Computational Measurement of Team-Process Phase Dynamics in Collaborative Virtual Reality
summary: Collaborative virtual reality (VR) environments make team communication observable as it unfolds, but conventional transcript analyses often summarize entire trials or divide them into fixed temporal windows. Such approaches can obscure changes in team communication and coordination over time. This article presents a computational framework for detecting and interpreting dynamic team-process phases from timestamped dialogue in a collaborative VR game. The framework uses late chunking to generate context-aware transcript representations, aggregates them into temporal chunks, and applies penalized Gaussian-kernel change-point detection to identify semantic transitions in team communication. After boundary detection, term frequency--inverse document frequency (TF-IDF), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), and representative transcript segments provide structured evidence for phase interpretation. A locally deployed large language model (LLM) uses in-context learning to generate initial interpretations that are subsequently reviewed by humans. Independently recorded interaction logs are then aligned with the detected phases to examine corresponding task-action patterns. The evaluation compares representations, pooling strategies, segmentation methods, parameter settings, reviewed phase interpretations, and phase-aligned interaction profiles. The results show that the framework identifies coherent and interpretable phase structures while preserving traceability to the underlying transcript evidence. The correspondence between transcript-derived phases and interaction behavior further supports their relevance for analyzing collaborative activity. The framework therefore offers a transparent and transferable approach for studying temporal changes in teamwork from timestamped transcripts across collaborative task settings.

AI.tldr: A computational framework for detecting dynamic team-process phases from timestamped VR dialogue using late chunking, change-point detection, and LLM-aided interpretation.
AI.motivation: Conventional transcript analyses summarize entire trials or use fixed windows, obscuring changes in team communication and coordination over time during collaborative VR activities.
AI.method: 1) Late chunking for context-aware transcript representations, 2) Aggregation into temporal chunks, 3) Penalized Gaussian-kernel change-point detection to identify semantic transitions, 4) TF-IDF, NMF, and representative segments for phase interpretation, 5) Locally deployed LLM for initial interpretations with human review, 6) Alignment with interaction logs.
AI.result: The framework identifies coherent and interpretable phase structures while preserving traceability to underlying transcript evidence. Correspondence between transcript-derived phases and interaction behavior supports their relevance for analyzing collaborative activity.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a transparent and transferable approach for studying temporal changes in teamwork from timestamped transcripts across collaborative task settings.

title: Candidate-Fate Accounting for Transparent Sensor Diagnostic Pipeline Search
summary: Industrial sensor diagnostics relies on preprocessing, representation, and classification pipelines, making automated pipeline search useful for reducing manual design cost. However, existing automated machine/deep learning (AutoML/AutoDL) reports typically retain only fitted trials, scores, and winners, omitting generated candidates that are invalid, pruned, skipped, cached, or unfitted. This omission limits reviewers' ability to check signal constraints, budget use, and unevaluated legal alternatives. To address this, we propose candidate-fate accounting, a candidate-level audit framework for diagnostic search traces. It records each observed candidate as auditable evidence: hashes merge repeated observations, legality checks flag invalid candidates, allocation rationales explain budget decisions, and a closed fate ledger assigns one terminal fate to each candidate. Experiments on three bearing-diagnostic datasets show that the framework detects invalid candidates and identifies 30--41 candidates omitted by fitted-trial-only reports, with closed fate records verifying complete candidate accounting while maintaining competitive diagnostic performance. The code is available at https://github.com/XXIE999/candidate-fate-accounting.

AI.tldr: Proposes candidate-fate accounting, an audit framework for AutoML/AutoDL pipeline search that tracks all candidate pipelines including invalid, pruned, skipped, cached, and unfitted ones, addressing limitations of conventional reports that only retain fitted trials.
AI.motivation: Existing AutoML/AutoDL reports for industrial sensor diagnostics only keep fitted trials, scores, and winners, omitting generated candidates that are invalid, pruned, skipped, cached, or unfitted. This omission prevents reviewers from checking signal constraints, budget use, and unevaluated legal alternatives, limiting auditability and transparency.
AI.method: Proposes candidate-fate accounting: a candidate-level audit framework that records each observed candidate as auditable evidence. Key components include: hashes to merge repeated observations, legality checks to flag invalid candidates, allocation rationales to explain budget decisions, and a closed fate ledger assigning one terminal fate to each candidate.
AI.result: Experiments on three bearing-diagnostic datasets show the framework detects invalid candidates and identifies 30-41 candidates omitted by fitted-trial-only reports. Closed fate records verify complete candidate accounting while maintaining competitive diagnostic performance comparable to conventional approaches.
AI.conclusion: Candidate-fate accounting provides transparent auditability for AutoML/AutoDL pipeline search in industrial sensor diagnostics, enabling comprehensive tracking of all candidate pipelines while preserving diagnostic accuracy, addressing limitations of conventional reporting methods.

title: Reinforced Planning with Latent World Models
summary: Humans solve complex problems by constructing plans and mentally simulating their outcomes with an internal model of the world. Machine learning has produced world models that similarly predict the outcomes of action sequences, but the improvement of candidate plans still isn't fully learned. Current planners are either hand-designed, distilled from a hand-designed optimizer, or learned only to inform an amortized policy rather than to revise the plan itself. We introduce the Reinforced Planning, a method based on the idea that search can be learned by reinforcing good search rules into a neural planner. Our implementation RP1 learns both how to evaluate imagined outcomes through a critic, as well as how to improve multi-step plans through an optimizer trained fully offline from imagined world-model roll-outs. To our knowledge, RP1 is the first method to fully learn how to improve multi-step plans. Furthermore, it can be trained independently of and attached to any pretrained latent world model. Across visual navigation, arm reaching, and robotic manipulation on two world-model backbones, RP1 substantially outperforms hand-designed search algorithms, reaching near-perfect success in several settings while using $1,000 \times$ less world-model rollouts and being up to $67 \times$ faster than the strongest alternative under concurrent planner inference.

AI.tldr: RP1 learns to improve multi-step plans through a learned planner trained offline from world-model rollouts, achieving better performance with fewer rollouts than hand-designed search algorithms.
AI.motivation: Current planners in machine learning are either hand-designed, distilled from hand-designed optimizers, or learned only to inform amortized policies rather than to revise plans themselves. There's a need for a method that fully learns how to improve multi-step plans.
AI.method: Reinforced Planning (RP1) learns both how to evaluate imagined outcomes through a critic and how to improve multi-step plans through an optimizer trained fully offline from imagined world-model roll-outs. It learns search by reinforcing good search rules into a neural planner.
AI.result: RP1 substantially outperforms hand-designed search algorithms across visual navigation, arm reaching, and robotic manipulation tasks. It achieves near-perfect success in several settings while using 1,000× less world-model rollouts and being up to 67× faster than the strongest alternative under concurrent planner inference.
AI.conclusion: RP1 is the first method to fully learn how to improve multi-step plans, and it can be trained independently of and attached to any pretrained latent world model, representing a significant advancement in learned planning.

title: Sanyu Studio: A Multi-Agent System for Art-Historical Narrative Construction
summary: Amid concerns that generative AI may standardize art interpretation, this paper examines whether LLM-based interaction can support plural art-historical narrative construction. We present Sanyu Studio, a multi-agent dialogue system that models 321 Sanyu oil paintings as agents with fact, interpretation, organization, and memory-filtering mechanisms. Based on a seven-day workshop with eight art-university participants, the study shows that user prompts, evidence organization, and cognitive tendencies shaped divergent yet coherent versions of digital Sanyu. The findings suggest that, under conditions of limited historical evidence, AI can amplify human agency and offer public audiences an interactive entry point into art-historical interpretation.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent dialogue system called Sanyu Studio enables users to construct plural art-historical narratives through LLM-based interaction with 321 Sanyu paintings modeled as intelligent agents, showing AI can amplify human agency rather than standardize interpretation.
AI.motivation: Addressing concerns that generative AI may standardize art interpretation, the paper investigates whether LLM-based interaction can instead support plural narrative construction in art history, offering an alternative to homogenized AI interpretations.
AI.method: Developed Sanyu Studio, a multi-agent dialogue system that models 321 Sanyu oil paintings as agents with four mechanisms (fact, interpretation, organization, and memory-filtering), then conducted a seven-day workshop with eight art-university participants to study narrative construction.
AI.result: User prompts, evidence organization, and cognitive tendencies shaped divergent yet coherent versions of digital Sanyu. The system enabled participants to construct personalized narratives while maintaining coherence with available historical evidence.
AI.conclusion: Under conditions of limited historical evidence, AI can amplify human agency rather than standardize interpretation. Such systems offer public audiences an interactive entry point into art-historical interpretation while preserving narrative pluralism.

title: An Empirical Benchmark of Deep Time-Series Models for Smart Meter Energy Forecasting
summary: Accurate forecasting of energy consumption is important for the efficient operation of power systems, with direct implications for operational costs, energy management, and system maintenance. Due to the availability of extensive high-resolution consumption data from smart meters, data-driven methods have been used for short-term and long-term forecasting. However, their comparative performance on real-world smart meter data is still not well studied. In this paper, we present an empirical benchmark of nine modern deep learning models for time-series forecasting, including linear, MLP-based, convolutional, and Transformer architectures. We evaluate these models on two publicly available smart meter datasets. Our analysis focuses on three factors that strongly affect forecasting performance: the length of historical input, the prediction horizon, and the choice of model architecture. We show that extending the historical context improves accuracy, but only up to a saturation point, after which additional input provides limited benefit. In contrast, accuracy decreases as the prediction horizon increases. We also investigate the trade-off between prediction accuracy and computational complexity, and assess the statistical significance and practical magnitude of performance differences across models. Our results show that deep learning models consistently outperform classical baselines, while lightweight architectures achieve relatively similar performance at significantly lower computational cost. Additionally, architectural differences only become meaningful at longer forecasting horizons and on more heterogeneous datasets. Finally, a subgroup analysis across geodemographic and household categories shows that model choice has limited impact for most population segments.

AI.tldr: Empirical benchmark study comparing 9 deep learning models for energy consumption forecasting on smart meter data, finding that extended historical context helps up to a saturation point, accuracy decreases with longer prediction horizons, and lightweight architectures achieve similar performance to complex ones at lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Energy consumption forecasting is crucial for efficient power system operation, affecting costs and maintenance. While extensive smart meter data enables data-driven forecasting, there's insufficient comparative analysis of modern deep learning models' performance on real-world smart meter data.
AI.method: Empirical benchmark of 9 deep learning models (linear, MLP-based, convolutional, Transformer architectures) evaluated on two publicly available smart meter datasets. Analysis focuses on three key factors: historical input length, prediction horizon, and model architecture choice.
AI.result: Extending historical context improves accuracy up to a saturation point; accuracy decreases with longer prediction horizons; deep learning models consistently outperform classical baselines; lightweight architectures achieve similar performance at significantly lower computational cost; architectural differences only matter at longer horizons and on more heterogeneous datasets; model choice has limited impact for most population segments.
AI.conclusion: The study provides practical guidance for model selection in energy forecasting, showing that simpler architectures can be as effective as complex ones, especially considering computational efficiency. Model choice should be tailored to specific forecasting horizons and dataset characteristics rather than always opting for the most complex architectures.

title: RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training
summary: Training multi-turn agentic workflows with reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models to perform complex reasoning, use external tools, and conduct iterative search beyond single-turn settings. Yet multi-turn RL training remains highly unstable, often causing severe performance degradation as the number of turns increases. Through theoretical analysis, we identify three tightly coupled sources of instability: rollout-training context mismatch, weak turn-level credit assignment under sparse terminal rewards, and asynchronous policy drift when short and long trajectories are optimized under different policy versions. We show that these issues share a common structural origin in flattened trajectory optimization and address them through a unified reverse-turn formulation. We propose Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization (RTPO), which organizes multi-turn rollouts as sparse reverse trees and performs turn-level policy updates in temporal reverse order, aligning each decision with its downstream continuation. RTPO enables causally consistent turn-level credit assignment and on-policy continuation to control asynchronous drift. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that RTPO eliminates context mismatch and asynchronous drift under the proposed turn-level formulation, reduces credit bias, and converges to recursive optimality. Experiments on multi-turn agentic RL benchmarks show that RTPO improves upon trajectory- and turn-level baselines by 21.50% and 10.76%, respectively, highlighting its potential to support more stable training for tool-using agents.

AI.tldr: RTPO (Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization) stabilizes multi-turn RL training for LLM agents by organizing rollouts as reverse trees and updating policies in temporal reverse order, addressing instability from context mismatch, poor credit assignment, and asynchronous policy drift.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn RL training for agentic workflows using large language models suffers from severe performance degradation and instability as the number of turns increases, which limits their ability to perform complex reasoning, use tools, and conduct iterative search effectively.
AI.method: Through theoretical analysis, identifies three sources of instability: rollout-training context mismatch, weak turn-level credit assignment under sparse rewards, and asynchronous policy drift. Proposes Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization (RTPO) that organizes multi-turn rollouts as sparse reverse trees and performs turn-level policy updates in temporal reverse order, aligning decisions with downstream continuation.
AI.result: RTPO provides theoretical guarantees eliminating context mismatch and asynchronous drift, reduces credit bias, and converges to recursive optimality. Experiments on multi-turn agentic RL benchmarks show improvements of 21.50% over trajectory-level baselines and 10.76% over turn-level baselines.
AI.conclusion: RTPO offers a unified solution to multi-turn RL instability through reverse-turn formulation, enabling more stable training for tool-using agents by addressing core structural problems in flattened trajectory optimization.

title: Transforming Heart Disease Prediction with Advanced Machine Learning Techniques
summary: Heart disease remains the leading cause of mortality globally, necessitating early and accurate detection to improve patient outcomes. This research focuses on the predictive analysis of heart disease using machine learning (ML) techniques, comparing the performance of multiple classifiers to identify the most accurate and least error-prone method. Two datasets from UCI and Kaggle repositories were utilized, each containing 14 attributes related to heart health indicators. Techniques including J48, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, Simple Cart, Bagging, Decision Stump, AdaBoost, Artificial Neural Networks, and Support Vector Machine (SVM) were applied. Evaluation metrics such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Relative Absolute Error (RAE), accuracy, precision, recall, and F-measure were used for performance comparison. Results revealed that SVM achieved the highest performance on the UCI dataset, while Simple Cart performed best on the Kaggle dataset, offering the highest accuracy and lowest error rates. The research work concludes that ML models, when properly tuned and validated, can significantly assist in the early diagnosis of heart disease, offering critical support for clinical decision-making. Future work may involve hybrid approaches and the use of more recent datasets to further improve prediction accuracy.

AI.tldr: ML models for heart disease prediction using multiple classifiers on UCI/Kaggle datasets; SVM performs best on UCI, Simple Cart best on Kaggle
AI.motivation: Heart disease is the leading global cause of mortality, requiring early and accurate detection to improve patient outcomes through better clinical decision-making.
AI.method: Used two datasets (UCI and Kaggle) with 14 heart health attributes each; applied multiple ML classifiers including J48, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, Simple Cart, Bagging, Decision Stump, AdaBoost, ANN, and SVM; evaluated using MAE, RAE, accuracy, precision, recall, and F-measure.
AI.result: SVM achieved highest performance on UCI dataset; Simple Cart performed best on Kaggle dataset with highest accuracy and lowest error rates.
AI.conclusion: Properly tuned and validated ML models can significantly assist in early heart disease diagnosis and support clinical decision-making; future work may involve hybrid approaches and newer datasets.

title: Competence, Not Accuracy: A Diagnostic for Reference-Free Judge Gates in Skill Optimization
summary: Text-space skill optimization adapts a frozen agent by evolving a natural-language skill document, accepting each candidate through a validation gate. Existing gates rely on verifiable rewards, confining these methods to tasks with an automatic verifier. Replacing the verifier with an LLM-judge gate would lift that restriction, but whether such a gate carries usable signal is untested. We ask a prior question: can we tell, before placing a judge in the loop, whether its scores separate correct from incorrect answers at all? We formalize a reference-free judge as a latent solver -- its verdict rests on agreement with whatever it would itself conclude, so its capacity to evaluate is bounded by its capacity to solve. The model yields a closed-form bound on discriminability (ROC-AUC) in the judge's competence $c$ and answer-space size $k$, a necessary condition $c > 1/k$, and the result that the marginal AUC is confounded by item difficulty while a within-question estimator is not. A non-intervening probe records judge scores on genuine optimization runs without altering any decision. We find discriminability at chance where competence sits near the floor and usable above it; that a judge's benchmark accuracy overstates the competence that matters; and, in a closed-loop study, that the screen predicts which kind of gating error occurs. The result is a cheap pre-deployment diagnostic for judge gates.

AI.tldr: Researchers analyze whether LLM judges can reliably evaluate text-based skill optimization by establishing a mathematical bound showing judges need basic competence to discriminate good from bad solutions, and provide a pre-deployment diagnostic.
AI.motivation: Current text-space skill optimization methods rely on automatic verifiers, limiting them to tasks with pre-defined rewards. Using LLM judges instead could expand applicability, but it's unknown whether their evaluation scores provide usable signals to separate correct from incorrect answers.
AI.method: Formalize reference-free LLM judges as latent solvers, derive mathematical bounds on discriminability (ROC-AUC) based on judge competence and answer-space size, propose a non-intervening probe to assess discriminability without altering optimization decisions, and validate through closed-loop studies.
AI.result: Established a necessary condition (judge competence > 1/k) for discriminability, found that benchmark accuracy overstates relevant competence, showed discriminability is at chance when competence is low but usable when above threshold, and demonstrated that proposed screen predicts gating error types in practice.
AI.conclusion: The analysis provides a cheap pre-deployment diagnostic tool to determine whether an LLM judge gate will work for text-space skill optimization before implementation, helping researchers avoid ineffective configurations and expanding potential applications beyond tasks with automatic verifiers.

title: Europe's Climate Ambition Under Scrutiny: Evidence from Deep Learning Emission Projections
summary: The European Union has committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions 55% below 1990 levels by 2030, but whether current trends are compatible with this ambition remains uncertain. We apply deep learning to high-resolution socioeconomic and sectoral data across EU27 member states till 2023 to project sectoral CO$_2$ trajectories under current trends, extrapolating observed sectoral momentum without assuming changes in the pace or effectiveness of the policy environment beyond what is already reflected in historical data. We project that EU27 emissions will exceed the 2030 target by 35% (620 Mt CO$_2$ shortfall), with only a small minority of countries on trajectories consistent with the bloc's commitments. While the Power sector achieves target-consistent reductions driven by the renewable transition, Mobility shows minimal progress and accounts for over a third of total emissions by 2030, reflecting a structural inertia across member states rather than geographically concentrated lag. Our findings indicate that substantial additional intervention is required to close Europe's ambition-implementation gap, and call for establishing up-to-date energy information in Europe.

AI.tldr: EU27 emissions projected to exceed 2030 climate target by 35% (620 Mt CO2) under current trends, with only Power sector on track while Mobility remains problematic.
AI.motivation: To assess whether current EU emission trends are compatible with the bloc's commitment to reduce greenhouse gases 55% below 1990 levels by 2030, given uncertainty about progress.
AI.method: Applied deep learning to high-resolution socioeconomic and sectoral data across EU27 member states up to 2023, projecting sectoral CO2 trajectories under current trends without assuming policy changes beyond what's already reflected in historical data.
AI.result: EU27 emissions projected to exceed 2030 target by 35% (620 Mt CO2 shortfall), with only small minority of countries on target-consistent trajectories. Power sector achieves target reductions driven by renewables, but Mobility shows minimal progress and accounts for over a third of total emissions by 2030, showing structural inertia across member states.
AI.conclusion: Substantial additional intervention is required to close Europe's ambition-implementation gap, and there's a need for establishing up-to-date energy information in Europe to track progress effectively.

title: A Multi-Agent Platform for Automated Enterprise Analytics and Insight Generation
summary: This paper proposes a multi-agent framework built on CrewAI [1] for conversational business intelligence. Five specialized AI agents operate in a sequential pipeline to process natural language queries, retrieve and analyze data, generate visualizations via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) [2], and deliver actionable insights. The platform features a defense-in-depth security architecture for multi-tenant data isolation and a query parameterization mechanism for transforming conversational insights into reusable dashboard components. Evaluation across 300 end-to-end test cases spanning synthetic and production enterprise datasets demonstrates 95.3% functional accuracy, a mean response latency of 24 seconds, and a response quality score of 4.52/5.0 as assessed by an LLM-as-a-Judge framework, with a 93.0% hallucination-free rate, representing a 22.6 percentage point accuracy improvement and 20.2% quality gain over a single-agent baseline. Cross-model evaluation across four LLM backends and human expert validation confirm architectural generalizability and evaluator reliability. An ablation study confirms that the Data Analysis and Report Aggregation agents are the primary drivers of output quality.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent CrewAI framework for conversational business intelligence with 5 specialized agents achieves 95.3% functional accuracy, 24-second latency, and 93% hallucination-free responses, showing significant improvements over single-agent baseline.
AI.motivation: To address limitations of single-agent systems in conversational business intelligence by creating a specialized multi-agent framework that can process natural language queries, analyze data, generate visualizations, and deliver actionable insights with higher accuracy and quality.
AI.method: Built on CrewAI with 5 specialized agents operating in sequential pipeline: natural language query processing, data retrieval, data analysis, visualization generation via Model Context Protocol (MCP), and insight delivery. Features defense-in-depth security architecture, multi-tenant data isolation, and query parameterization for reusable dashboard components.
AI.result: 95.3% functional accuracy across 300 test cases, 24-second mean latency, 4.52/5.0 response quality score, 93.0% hallucination-free rate. Shows 22.6 percentage point accuracy improvement and 20.2% quality gain over single-agent baseline. Ablation study identifies Data Analysis and Report Aggregation agents as primary quality drivers.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent framework effectively addresses conversational business intelligence challenges, demonstrating superior performance over single-agent systems. The architecture is generalizable across LLM backends, and the defense-in-depth security makes it suitable for enterprise multi-tenant environments.

title: Multi-Class Electrical and Mechanical Fault Classification Using Random Convolutional Kernels
comment: Interdisciplinary Conference on Electrics and Computer (INTCEC 2026)
summary: Diagnosing faults in rotating machinery is essential for ensuring the reliability of industrial processes. Random convolutional kernel-based Time Series Classification (TSC) methods, such as ROCKET and its variants, provide an attractive trade-off between predictive performance and computational efficiency. In this work, we evaluate SelF-Rocket for the multi-class diagnosis of both mechanical and electrical faults and introduce, as a new contribution, a multivariate extension of the original method. The proposed approach is compared with leading ROCKET-based methods on two public benchmark datasets, MaFaulDa (mechanical faults) and ITSC-UDG (stator inter-turn short circuits), under both univariate and multivariate settings. Experimental results show that SelF-Rocket achieves the best overall accuracy-latency trade-off among the evaluated methods, obtaining the highest classification performance on MaFaulDa while remaining highly competitive on the more challenging ITSC-UDG dataset.

AI.tldr: SelF-Rocket, a random convolutional kernel-based time series classification method, is extended to multivariate settings and shows superior accuracy-latency trade-off for rotating machinery fault diagnosis compared to other ROCKET-based methods.
AI.motivation: Fault diagnosis in rotating machinery is critical for industrial reliability. While ROCKET-based methods offer good performance-efficiency balance, there's a need to evaluate their effectiveness for multi-class fault diagnosis in both mechanical and electrical faults, particularly in multivariate settings.
AI.method: The paper evaluates SelF-Rocket for multi-class fault diagnosis and introduces a multivariate extension of the original method. The approach is benchmarked against leading ROCKET-based methods on two public datasets (MaFaulDa for mechanical faults and ITSC-UDG for stator inter-turn short circuits) under both univariate and multivariate settings.
AI.result: SelF-Rocket achieves the best overall accuracy-latency trade-off among evaluated methods. It obtains the highest classification performance on the MaFaulDa dataset while remaining highly competitive on the more challenging ITSC-UDG dataset.
AI.conclusion: SelF-Rocket provides an effective solution for rotating machinery fault diagnosis with superior performance-efficiency characteristics, especially when extended to multivariate scenarios, making it suitable for practical industrial applications.

title: Metrics That Write Themselves: Evolving an Evaluator from Its Own Blind Spots
summary: Agents improve quickly against a reliable automatic metric and stall without one, and the applications that need them most, report generation among them, are the ones nobody knows how to score. Can the metric write itself? Saying what makes an answer good is hard; pointing at something wrong with one is easier, so the metric we evolve is a pool of small Python operators that each flag a candidate for one named defect, or abstain, and vote. Asking a model for operators directly does not work: 183 candidates realise only 96 distinct behaviours, from one narrow region of an enormous space. EvalCEGAR instead borrows counterexample-guided abstraction refinement from program verification. It reads the pool as an abstraction and searches for a collision, two answers the operators score identically, one correct and one not. That pair, not a prompt, is the authoring request, and when a collision defeats every attempt the loop widens what an operator may read rather than resampling. On MBPP+ and HumanEval+, a sandbox whose hidden unit tests give exact ground truth, the loop writes a 55-line operator that closes 15.4% of the gap between flagging nothing and a perfect filter on 428 unseen tasks (+0.0065, p=0.0010) at a quarter of our best hand-written operator's flags. On the benchmark it never saw it matches that operator's effect exactly on a third of the flags. Six of eight runs admit such an operator and all six help out of sample; our 15 hand-written operators applied together as one filter lose accuracy. An LLM judge on the same information ties that delta on a nearly disjoint set of candidates, and charges a model call per candidate forever where the operator charges none.

AI.tldr: An automated method called EvalCEGAR evolves small Python operators that flag defects in AI-generated answers, achieving significant performance improvements on coding benchmarks without requiring model calls per candidate.
AI.motivation: Agents need reliable automatic metrics to improve, but many important applications like report generation lack good scoring methods. Traditional approaches struggle because saying what makes an answer good is hard, but pointing out defects is easier.
AI.method: EvalCEGAR borrows counterexample-guided abstraction refinement from program verification. It evolves a pool of small Python operators that each flag a specific defect or abstain, then votes. The system searches for collisions (answers scored identically but one correct, one not) and uses these pairs to author new operators, widening what operators can read when collisions defeat all attempts.
AI.result: On MBPP+ and HumanEval+, EvalCEGAR produces a 55-line operator that closes 15.4% of the performance gap between no filtering and perfect filtering on 428 unseen tasks (+0.0065, p=0.0010), using only 1/4 of the flags of the best hand-written operator. The operator generalizes to unseen benchmarks, matching hand-written performance on a third of flags. Six of eight runs produce useful operators, while hand-written operators lose accuracy when combined.
AI.conclusion: Automatically evolving defect-detection operators through counterexample-guided refinement provides an effective, low-cost alternative to both manual operator writing and LLM-based judging, offering significant performance improvements without the ongoing computational cost of model calls per candidate.

title: Visual-Aware Representation of Web Pages for Machine Learning Applications
summary: Applying machine learning to web pages is challenging due to the need to interpret HTML together with associated resources and perform rendering to obtain a meaningful visual and layout-aware representation. As a result, machine learning over web content remains comparatively underexplored. In this paper, we present a platform for visual-aware representation and machine learning over web pages based on the open-source rendering tool FitLayout. The platform provides a server capable of rendering web pages, explicitly capturing their visual and structural properties in an RDF-based representation, and persisting the rendered documents in an integrated storage. The processing pipeline is controlled via a REST API, while SPARQL queries are used to retrieve structured data suitable as input for machine learning algorithms. By explicitly modeling rendered web pages, including fine-grained layout details, the platform enables dataset sharing and supports the reproducibility of experimental results. The architecture supports the complete dataset preparation workflow, from web page collection and rendering through preprocessing and annotation of content elements to downstream learning tasks. We further provide a Python client library that integrates the platform with standard machine learning workflows. As a demonstration, we show how rendered web pages can be transformed into graph-based representations and used to train graph neural networks for recognizing key content elements, illustrating both the applicability of the approach and the reproducibility of the results.

AI.tldr: A platform for visual-aware machine learning on web pages using HTML rendering to capture layout and visual properties, enabling reproducible web content analysis through graph-based representations.
AI.motivation: Machine learning on web content is challenging because it requires interpreting HTML with associated resources and rendering to obtain meaningful visual and layout-aware representations, making this area comparatively underexplored.
AI.method: Developed a platform based on FitLayout rendering tool that includes: 1) a server for rendering web pages and capturing visual/structural properties in RDF-based representation, 2) integrated storage for rendered documents, 3) REST API for pipeline control, 4) SPARQL queries for structured data retrieval, and 5) Python client library for ML workflow integration.
AI.result: Created a complete dataset preparation workflow supporting web page collection, rendering, preprocessing, annotation, and downstream learning tasks. Demonstrated transformation of rendered web pages into graph-based representations for training graph neural networks to recognize key content elements.
AI.conclusion: The platform enables explicit modeling of rendered web pages with fine-grained layout details, supporting dataset sharing and reproducibility of experimental results while providing a practical approach for visual-aware machine learning on web content.

title: Pairwise Logical Selection of Enthymeme Completions under Semantic-Link Uncertainty
summary: Arguments often omit premises or claims, forming enthymemes. We study pairwise logical selection between two candidates for the omitted component. Existing natural language methods can identify or generate candidates but often do not expose how the selected candidate completes the inference, while logic-based approaches usually assume that the required formulae and background knowledge are available. We extend a prior neuro-symbolic pipeline from missing-premise to missing-claim selection and replace binary entailment outcomes with logical-resistance scores. Top-Link uses weighted Partial MaxSAT under a single configuration of highest-confidence semantic links. We then introduce Possible-World Atom-Link Formalization (PWAL), which keeps translated formulae fixed and marginalizes logical resistance over alternative cross-formula semantic-link configurations. We evaluate PWAL on five tasks: ARCT and a CDED-derived task for missing-premise selection, iDebate- and AAE2-derived tasks for missing-claim selection, and alphaNLI for abductive hypothesis selection. Relative to Top-Link, PWAL raises strict accuracy by 2.95-30.86 percentage points and reduces tie rates by 4.57-58.00 percentage points on all five tasks. When ties receive half credit, accuracy still increases by 0.45-6.04 percentage points. PWAL also records the translated formulae, sampled link configurations, and resistance components for every comparison, providing a transparent trace of each score.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic approach called PWAL improves logical selection in enthymemes by marginalizing over semantic link configurations, outperforming existing methods on five different missing-premise and missing-claim tasks.
AI.motivation: Real-world arguments often omit premises or claims (enthymemes), creating incomplete inferences. Existing approaches have limitations: natural language methods don't explain how selected components complete inferences, while logic-based methods assume all needed formulae and background knowledge are available.
AI.method: Extends prior neuro-symbolic pipeline from missing-premise to missing-claim selection, replacing binary entailment with logical-resistance scores. Introduces Possible-World Atom-Link Formalization (PWAL) which keeps translated formulae fixed and marginalizes logical resistance over alternative cross-formula semantic-link configurations. Compares with Top-Link approach that uses weighted Partial MaxSAT under single highest-confidence semantic link configuration.
AI.result: PWAL outperforms Top-Link on five tasks: raises strict accuracy by 2.95-30.86 percentage points, reduces tie rates by 4.57-58.00 percentage points. Even when ties receive half credit, accuracy increases by 0.45-6.04 percentage points. Provides transparent trace of each score through recorded formulae, link configurations, and resistance components.
AI.conclusion: PWAL offers a robust neuro-symbolic framework for logical selection in enthymemes that significantly improves accuracy, reduces tie rates, and provides transparency through detailed traceability of scoring decisions.

title: FedLNS: Leverage LayerNorm Signature Modeling to Mitigate Adversarial Manipulation in Federated LLMs
summary: Federated training enables language models to learn from distributed private text, but the server cannot directly verify the local supervision or optimization process that produces each client update. A malicious client can therefore train on corrupted targets, introduce incorrect context-token associations, and degrade the global model through repeated aggregation. Such degradation can also increase the risk of unreliable or hallucinatory generation. We propose Federated Learning with Normalization Signatures (FedLNS), a server-side framework for lightweight malicious-update screening. FedLNS represents each client update through changes in trainable normalization-layer parameters and screens suspicious updates against a robust, history-aware cross-client reference. Because the signatures are extracted at the server from the returned local models, FedLNS requires no additional client-to-server parameter or metadata exchange compared to standard federated learning (FL) methods. After screening, the retained full-model updates can be aggregated using standard FL or another compatible aggregation rule. FedLNS requires no raw client data, trusted server dataset, labeled attack examples, or separately trained detector. Experiments on GPT-style, BERT-style, and LLaMA-style models trained from scratch with 200 clients show that, under 40% population-level target manipulation, FedLNS achieves lower test perplexity than the strongest of six baselines for all three architectures under both IID (independently and identically distributed) and non-IID data partitions.

AI.tldr: FedLNS is a server-side framework for detecting malicious client updates in federated learning by analyzing normalization-layer parameter changes and screening them against cross-client references, without needing additional client data or trusted datasets.
AI.motivation: Federated learning of language models faces security risks where malicious clients can introduce corrupted training data, create incorrect context-token associations, and degrade global model quality through repeated aggregation, potentially leading to unreliable or hallucinatory generation.
