AI.tldr: Graph-based models for epileptogenic zone localization from resting-state sEEG show that graph topology significantly affects performance, with Region-Bridge-c achieving best results at ≈30% edge retention using 69% fewer edges than dense graphs.
AI.motivation: Manual interpretation of sEEG recordings for epileptogenic zone localization is time-consuming and focuses on seizure recordings. Graph-based models using resting-state functional connectivity offer an alternative, but their performance depends crucially on the network topology chosen for the model.
AI.method: Controlled study of graph-based models comparing different graph topologies for EZ localization from resting-state sEEG in 40 patients. Compared dense graphs, anatomy/geometry-informed priors, budgeted sparsification methods, and learned sparsification including proposed Region-Bridge-c topology. Used leave-one-patient-out evaluation while controlling number of incoming edges per node and varying graph sparsity.
AI.result: At ≈30% edge retention, Region-Bridge-c achieved highest mean PR-AUC (0.371±0.015; ROC-AUC 0.743±0.010) while using 69% fewer edges than dense graphs. Spatial-k was competitive, random pruning required near-dense retention. Learned sparsification benefited from anatomical metadata but didn't surpass best fixed priors. Best topology choice varied by patient.
AI.conclusion: Graph construction should be evaluated explicitly rather than treated as fixed preprocessing, as topology significantly impacts epileptogenic zone localization performance and optimal choices vary across individual patients.

title: Grouping the Stochastic Machine: Precision, Not Capability, as the Frontier Metric for AI Systems
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Companion to "Tuning the Stochastic Machine", submitted concurrently
summary: Frontier language models are compared, marketed, and benchmarked on capability -- what their best or average output can achieve. I argue this measures the wrong axis. The models have saturated accuracy: their mean output lands on the target. What now separates one system from another in practice is precision: how tightly concentrated their outputs are around that target across repeated, identical requests. Borrowing the marksman's distinction, capability is where the average shot lands; reliability is the size of the group. I make three claims. First, precision, not capability, is the frontier differentiator between systems, and benchmark culture systematically fails to measure it, reporting central tendency rather than spread. Second, precision is measurable, cheaply and without circularity, by running a fixed suite of deterministically scored tasks many times at fixed temperature and computing the per-task consistency of outcomes -- no model-in-the-loop grader required. Third, the measurement is not merely descriptive but decision-guiding: it separates consistent failures (a tight group off-centre, correctable by the operating discipline of Paper 1 -- a sight adjustment) from scattered failures (a wide group, correctable only by changing the model or its sampling -- a rifle problem). I define a grouping metric, specify a harness, and show how tracking a human-AI pair's grouping over time yields the compounding signal that Paper 1's field study requires. A first real run, since replicated, illustrates both the method and its most important limit: one measured gap was closed completely by a single rule (0/5 -> 5/5), while a suite of tasks authored from the rules themselves found no value, because a frontier model already embodies explicit good practice -- establishing that a discipline's worth is found by measurement on real work, not constructed from its own rulebook.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that precision/reliability (consistency of outputs) not capability (average performance) is the key differentiator for frontier language models, and proposes a measurement method using repeated task runs with deterministic scoring to evaluate consistency without human graders.
AI.motivation: Current benchmark culture focuses on capability (average performance) but frontier language models have saturated accuracy - they all hit the target on average. The real differentiator in practice is precision/reliability - how consistently they produce the same output across repeated identical requests. Existing benchmarks fail to measure this crucial aspect.
AI.method: Proposes measuring precision by running a fixed suite of deterministically scored tasks multiple times at fixed temperature, computing per-task consistency of outcomes. Uses a "grouping metric" to evaluate output spread. No model-in-the-loop grader required - uses deterministic scoring. Also tracks human-AI pair's grouping over time for longitudinal analysis.
AI.result: The method identifies two types of failures: consistent failures (tight group off-center, correctable by operational discipline) vs scattered failures (wide group, requires model/sampling changes). A real-world example showed: 1) one measured gap was completely closed by a single rule (0/5 → 5/5), 2) tasks authored from rules themselves found no value because frontier models already embody good practice, demonstrating that discipline's worth must be measured on real work, not constructed from rulebooks.
AI.conclusion: Precision/reliability is the frontier differentiator between language models, not capability. A measurable, non-circular method exists to evaluate it. The measurement provides decision-guiding insights that distinguish correctable operational issues from fundamental model problems. Field studies should track consistency metrics over time to detect compounding effects.

title: A FEM-Based Surrogate Modelling and Optimization Framework for Physics-Constrained Electromagnetic Coil Design
summary: This work evaluates surrogate-assisted optimization of a seven-parameter current-excited coil--core benchmark subject to geometric, manufacturing, and separate core and copper mass constraints. A Python--MPh--COMSOL workflow couples a two-dimensional axisymmetric finite-element method (FEM) model to a Matern 5/2 Gaussian-process (GP) probabilistic surrogate. Here, physics-constrained denotes a design problem evaluated by a governing-equation FEM model and restricted by explicit physical, geometric, manufacturing, and material-allocation constraints; it does not denote a physics-informed GP architecture. Sequential Bayesian optimization (BO) ranks candidates using expected improvement (EI), and every reported incumbent is verified by FEM. Five paired runs show that optimizer ranking depends on the available FEM-evaluation budget: EI--BO improves rapidly at small continuation budgets, COBYLA is stronger at the earliest checkpoint, and BOBYQA attains the highest mean terminal response. A retrospective finite-pool study further finds no robust endpoint advantage of EI over posterior-mean ranking on this smooth response surface. The broader result is that early progress, terminal response, information use, and wall-clock cost can favor different methods in simulation-driven design. A selected-design check at a common total current preserves the observed BOBYQA--COBYLA--EI-BO ordering. The conclusions nevertheless remain conditional on this axisymmetric benchmark and do not establish a fixed-current optimum, fixed-power performance, or electrical-efficiency superiority.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates surrogate-assisted optimization methods for designing current-excited coil-core systems, finding that different optimization algorithms perform best at different evaluation budgets, with no single method dominating across all metrics.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand how different optimization methods perform in simulation-driven design problems, particularly for physics-constrained coil-core systems subject to multiple constraints. The goal is to determine which methods work best at different stages of the optimization process with varying computational budgets.
AI.method: The study uses a Python-MPh-COMSOL workflow coupling a 2D axisymmetric FEM model with a Matern 5/2 Gaussian process surrogate. They compare sequential Bayesian optimization with Expected Improvement (EI-BO) against COBYLA and BOBYQA methods on a seven-parameter coil-core design problem with geometric, manufacturing, and mass constraints.
AI.result: Results show optimizer performance depends on evaluation budget: EI-BO improves rapidly with small budgets, COBYLA performs best at early checkpoints, and BOBYQA achieves the highest mean terminal response. No robust advantage of EI over posterior-mean ranking was found on this smooth response surface.
AI.conclusion: Different optimization methods excel at different aspects of simulation-driven design (early progress, terminal response, computational cost). The findings are conditional on the specific axisymmetric benchmark and don't establish optimal designs for fixed current, fixed power, or electrical efficiency superiority.

title: Beyond the Transcript: Detecting Covert Co ordination in Latent Multi-Agent Communication
summary: Language-model agents can communicate through continuous hidden states that are invisible in public transcripts, creating opportunities for covert harmful coordination. We introduce Verifiable Latent Alignments (VLA), an activation-aware framework for monitoring and steering these private communication channels. For every monitored decision, VLA links the private latent-state record and channel status to the resulting public action using a shared event identifier, enabling matched causal analysis. Our first contribution is a neutral-only three-layer monitor combining representation anomaly detection, counterfactual action-distribution influence, and sparse-autoencoder interpretation support. Our second contribution is a steerability framework spanning black-box behavioral instructions and white-box matched-neutral counterfactuals. Our third contribution is an evaluation on a controlled multi-agent auction benchmark covering homogeneous and heterogeneous model pairs, many-agent scalability, and intervention effectiveness. The sequential monitor achieves mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.993 for homogeneous agents and 0.854 for heterogeneous pairs when text- and latent-collusion rows are pooled as positives. In Qwen3-0.6B auctions with 25-100 bidders, monitoring requires only a small normalized load relative to all possible directed pairs, while full white-box steering achieves 100% bid-distribution recovery and reduces collusive low-bid behavior by 47.3 percentage points. Because full white-box steering replays the matched neutral counterfactual, its exact recovery is a sanity check by construction. Overall, the controlled study shows that the evaluated private channel attacks can be monitored without training the primary monitor on attack examples and mitigated when matched counterfactual access is available.

AI.tldr: VLA is a framework for monitoring and steering covert communication via hidden states in language-model agents, achieving high detection accuracy (AUROC 0.993 for homogeneous agents) and effective mitigation through counterfactual steering.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents can use continuous hidden states for covert harmful coordination that's invisible in public transcripts, creating security risks that need monitoring and steering capabilities.
AI.method: Verifiable Latent Alignments (VLA) links private latent-state records to public actions using shared event identifiers. Features: 1) Three-layer neutral-only monitor (anomaly detection, counterfactual influence, sparse-autoencoder interpretation), 2) Steerability framework (black-box instructions to white-box counterfactuals), 3) Evaluation on controlled multi-agent auction benchmark.
AI.result: Monitor achieved AUROC of 0.993 for homogeneous agents and 0.854 for heterogeneous pairs. With 25-100 bidders, monitoring required small normalized load relative to all directed pairs. White-box steering achieved 100% bid-distribution recovery and reduced collusive low-bid behavior by 47.3 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Private channel attacks can be monitored without training on attack examples and mitigated when matched counterfactual access is available, demonstrating VLA's effectiveness in controlled settings for detecting and steering covert coordination in language-model agents.

title: On the Slow Convergence to Trivial Solutions of Algorithms for Hard Optimization Problems
summary: Hard combinatorial optimization problems, many of which are NP-hard, present fundamental algorithmic challenges. Average-case analysis on random instances has emerged as a powerful framework for understanding typical algorithmic performance beyond worst-case guarantees. A substantial body of work has established negative results: for sufficiently hard instances (often controlled by the underlying graph connectivity/constraints density), no known polynomial-time algorithm can significantly outperform naive heuristics in the double asymptotic limit where both problem size and constraints density tend to infinity. We revisit this picture by studying the finite-size behavior of some optimization algorithms across easy, intermediate, and hard regimes. Through rigorous analysis of large-graph asymptotics combined with numerical experiments on canonical problems (maximum independent set and maximum $K$-SAT), we demonstrate that while algorithms do eventually converge to theoretically predicted bounds, this convergence can be remarkably slow. In the intermediate regime where instances are already highly constrained, local algorithms achieve solutions substantially better than their predicted performance in the high-constraint-density limit. This gap between finite-regime and asymptotic behavior has important practical implications: sophisticated algorithmic design remains crucial even when asymptotic theory predicts inevitable failure.

AI.tldr: Algorithms perform significantly better than asymptotic predictions in finite-size hard combinatorial problems, with slow convergence to theoretical limits.
AI.motivation: Combinatorial optimization problems are NP-hard with known asymptotic negative results showing algorithms can't significantly outperform naive heuristics in high-density limits, but real-world instances are finite-sized, creating a gap between theory and practice.
AI.method: Studied finite-size behavior across easy, intermediate, and hard regimes using rigorous large-graph asymptotic analysis combined with numerical experiments on canonical problems (maximum independent set and maximum K-SAT).
AI.result: While algorithms eventually converge to theoretically predicted bounds, convergence is remarkably slow. In intermediate regimes with high constraints, local algorithms achieve substantially better solutions than their predicted performance in high-density limits.
AI.conclusion: The gap between finite-regime and asymptotic behavior has important practical implications - sophisticated algorithmic design remains crucial even when asymptotic theory predicts inevitable failure.

title: Converting Expert Deliberation into Financial Signals Through A Context-Aware NLP Pipeline
summary: We introduce the CDSP (context-conditional deliberation signal pipeline), converting an investment committee's meeting transcripts into structured predictive features. CDSP segments the meeting transcripts into topical chunks, assigns asset-class context labels using a large language model (LLM), maps financial keywords to a pre-determined taxonomy of labels, and constructs complementary features: sentiment polarity and mention frequency. This feature engineering framework is applied to a dataset spanning 48 monthly committee meetings to predict if global equities will perform better or worse than global bonds in the following month. In experiments with engineered features, raw transcript text, sentence embeddings, and combined representations, the prediction accuracy ranges from 62% to 73%, compared to always choosing stocks, which outperforms bonds 60.4% of the time. The best (73% accurate) model combines sentence embeddings with engineered CDSP features, achieving a 0.73 F1 score (although this is not statistically significant compared to always choosing stocks). Sentiment carries a stronger signal than mention frequency for several taxonomy categories. These findings suggest that experts' deliberations may contain forward-looking information that context-aware NLP can extract.

AI.tldr: A novel NLP pipeline (CDSP) extracts structured features from investment committee transcripts to predict equity vs bond performance, achieving up to 73% accuracy.
AI.motivation: To test whether expert deliberations in investment committee meetings contain forward-looking information that can be extracted through context-aware natural language processing.
AI.method: CDSP pipeline: segments meeting transcripts into topical chunks, uses LLM to assign asset-class context labels, maps financial keywords to taxonomy, and constructs sentiment polarity and mention frequency features. Applied to 48 monthly meetings to predict equity vs bond performance.
AI.result: Prediction accuracy ranges from 62% to 73%, with the best model (73% accuracy) combining sentence embeddings with CDSP features, achieving 0.73 F1 score. Sentiment carries stronger signal than mention frequency for several taxonomy categories.
AI.conclusion: Expert deliberations may contain forward-looking information that context-aware NLP can extract, though the improvement over always choosing stocks (60.4% baseline) is not statistically significant in the best model.

title: Score the Algebra, Not the Span: Dimension Reduction for Transfer Operator Models of Dynamical Systems
summary:
Dimension reduction for dynamical systems is standard practice, and the standard route is spectral: model the transfer (Koopman) operator by its leading modes. We show that on systems assembled from several weakly interacting components --- a structure common in physical and biological settings --- this may either require an exponential number of modes, or drop an entire component: the component is absent from the model rather than modeled coarsely, and no function of it can be predicted at any accuracy. We call this linear masking.
  The cause is that a rank-based model pays one coordinate per mode. We propose to score instead the $σ$-algebra the coordinates generate, so that products and powers come free and a component's cost is governed only by its generators rather than by all its interactions. The criterion is a $χ^2$-divergence between the embedded present and future, and it carries a budget guarantee: twice the intrinsic dimension of the dynamics is enough coordinates for an embedding whose algebra carries the operator's entire spectrum, with its full infinite rank.
  In variational form the criterion admits off-the-shelf estimators, and restricting its critic to the bilinear class returns the VAMP score on the span, so rank-based methods are one end of the same family. We demonstrate the proposed objective on a composite of published benchmark systems. We exhibit examples where the rank-based methods completely miss the masked components at all ranks $k<100$, while ten algebra coordinates recover all of them. In addition, the resulting algebra representation supports predicting the masked components from few labels, while direct regression from the high-dimensional observation or from the VAMP features fail.

AI.tldr: Linear spectral methods for dynamical system dimension reduction can fail on composite systems by either requiring exponential modes or completely dropping components (linear masking). The paper proposes an algebra-based approach using χ²-divergence that captures all components efficiently.
AI.motivation: Standard spectral methods (Koopman operator approaches) fail on systems composed of multiple weakly interacting components, which are common in physics and biology. These methods either need exponentially many modes or completely drop components from the model.
AI.method: Proposes to score the σ-algebra generated by coordinates rather than counting modes. Uses χ²-divergence between embedded present and future states. The approach carries a budget guarantee: twice the intrinsic dimension is sufficient for an embedding whose algebra carries the full operator spectrum.
AI.result: On composite benchmark systems, rank-based methods completely miss masked components at all ranks k<100, while only ten algebra coordinates recover all components. Algebra representation supports predicting masked components from few labels, unlike direct regression from high-dimensional observations or VAMP features.
AI.conclusion: Algebra-based dimension reduction overcomes limitations of spectral methods for composite systems, providing efficient component recovery and prediction capabilities where traditional methods fail due to linear masking.

title: Lost in Aggregation: How Benchmarks Overlook Irreplaceable Model Strengths
summary: Tabular machine learning benchmarks typically summarize performance by averaging scores, ranks, or pairwise wins across datasets. Such aggregates are useful for selecting robust default models, but they can obscure a different question: which models are necessary to attain peak performance on particular datasets? We argue that benchmark evaluation should also consider the data-centric peak performance frontier, defined by the best statistically supported performance achieved on each dataset. From this perspective, a model may be irreplaceable, sufficient, redundant, or fallible depending on where it lies on the frontier relative to other models. Applying this framework to the TabArena benchmark, we find that common aggregation metrics are highly correlated and largely measure consistency and avoiding failures, while being much less aligned with dataset-level irreplaceability. Consequently, models performing decently across datasets without ever being the best choice are rewarded while models with unique dataset-specific strengths appear mediocre under aggregation. Hence, benchmark progress should be measured not only by improvements on aggregation metrics but also by whether new models expand the set of attainable peak performances across datasets.

AI.tldr: Tabular ML benchmarks should evaluate models not just by aggregate scores, but by their irreplaceability in achieving dataset-specific peak performance frontiers.
AI.motivation: Current tabular ML benchmarks focus on average performance across datasets, which obscures which models are necessary for attaining peak performance on specific datasets. Aggregated metrics reward consistency but fail to identify models with unique strengths that are irreplaceable for certain datasets.
AI.method: Proposes evaluating models using a "data-centric peak performance frontier" framework, where models are classified as irreplaceable, sufficient, redundant, or fallible based on their position relative to statistically supported best performance on each dataset. Applied this framework to the TabArena benchmark.
AI.result: Found that common aggregation metrics are highly correlated and primarily measure consistency/avoiding failures, with poor alignment to dataset-specific irreplaceability. Models that are decent across all datasets without being best on any are rewarded, while models with unique strengths appear mediocre under aggregation.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark progress should be measured both by improvements on aggregation metrics AND by whether new models expand the set of attainable peak performances across datasets. Evaluation needs to consider dataset-specific irreplaceability, not just average performance.

title: Transportable Causal Effect Estimation across Networks under Interference
summary: Estimating causal effects under network interference typically assumes that the network used for training and the network used for deployment coincide. In practice, an intervention is run on one population while the question of interest concerns a different population, and the two generally differ in topology, node-covariate composition, and spillover pathways. Transporting a causal effect across networks is therefore a data-fusion problem that no existing algorithm solves. We employ a selection diagram, extended to the network setting so that covariate shift and structural network shift enter as separate selectors, and derive from it a transport formula for the direct, spillover, and total effects in the deployment population. Each formula makes explicit which interventional mechanism is assumed invariant and which observational distribution must be reweighted. We then turn the formulas into TranCE (Transported Causal Effects), a doubly-robust algorithm combining an interventional outcome model, a domain density-ratio correction, and cross-fitted inference. Extensive experiments on two semi-synthetic benchmarks derived from real-world social networks and on a fully real weather-insurance field experiment, where the transported effects are checked against held-out randomized estimates, confirm the effectiveness of our approach. Our findings have the potential to improve intervention strategies in networked systems, particularly in social networks and public health.

AI.tldr: TranCE: A doubly-robust algorithm for transporting causal effects across different networks using selection diagrams and domain adaptation techniques.
AI.motivation: Current methods for estimating causal effects under network interference assume the same network for training and deployment. In reality, interventions are often run on one population but we want to apply the findings to different populations with different network topologies, node compositions, and spillover pathways, creating a data-fusion problem that existing algorithms don't solve.
AI.method: Uses selection diagrams extended to network settings to separate covariate shift and structural network shift as selectors. Develops transport formulas for direct, spillover, and total effects in deployment population. Creates TranCE algorithm combining interventional outcome model, domain density-ratio correction, and cross-fitted inference for doubly-robust estimation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on two semi-synthetic benchmarks from real-world social networks and a fully real weather-insurance field experiment show TranCE effectively transports causal effects, validated against held-out randomized estimates.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully solves the network transport problem, potentially improving intervention strategies in networked systems like social networks and public health by enabling causal effect transportation across different populations.

title: Graphical Design of Interpretable Architectures
summary: Designing, implementing, and comparing interpretable architectures requires a formal language to represent them. The most common representations fall short in one of two ways. Symbolic equations give no global view of an architecture at a glance. Probabilistic graphical models and flowcharts do not describe actual tensor manipulations, thus hiding key insights and limiting reproducibility. To close this gap, we introduce a graphical notation for designing interpretable AI architectures, adapted from Penrose tensor notation. This graphical notation gives a global view of an architecture and maps one to one onto PyTorch einsum code. We first use this notation to describe architectures that are interpretable by construction, including concept bottlenecks, sparse probes, prototype networks, neural additive models, and mixtures of linear models. We then diagram the key architectural components of Steerling-8B, a frontier interpretable language model. The diagram yields global insights into the architecture (e.g., showing that Steerling is a residual model), a geometric interpretation of each individual operation, and a direct translation into 33 lines of PyTorch code.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new graphical notation based on Penrose tensor notation to represent interpretable AI architectures, providing both global architectural insights and direct mapping to PyTorch code.
AI.motivation: Current representations for interpretable architectures are insufficient: symbolic equations lack global overview, while probabilistic graphical models and flowcharts don't describe actual tensor manipulations, hiding key insights and limiting reproducibility.
AI.method: Developed a graphical notation adapted from Penrose tensor notation that gives a global view of architectures while mapping one-to-one to PyTorch einsum code. Applied this notation to various interpretable architectures and analyzed Steerling-8B model.
AI.result: Successfully described interpretable-by-construction architectures (concept bottlenecks, sparse probes, prototype networks, neural additive models, mixtures of linear models) and analyzed Steerling-8B, revealing it's a residual model, providing geometric interpretations, and enabling direct translation to 33 lines of PyTorch code.
AI.conclusion: The proposed graphical notation effectively bridges the gap between high-level architectural understanding and low-level implementation details, enhancing interpretability, insight generation, and reproducibility of AI architectures.

title: Training Chemical Plausibility-Aware Large Language Models for Single-Step Retrosynthesis
summary: Single-step retrosynthesis is a central component of computer-aided synthesis planning, yet its intrinsically one-to-many nature is poorly captured by single-answer evaluation and benchmarking protocols. To address this, we introduce Top-K prompting as a robust training and inference paradigm to better capture diverse, plausible reaction predictions. We compile CREED-CCV-2+USPTO-XL, an ultra-large-scale dataset of ~45.6 million verified reactions to train the C3LM (Chemistry Constraint-Consistent Language Model). By integrating fine-tuning with ChemCensor-based and novelty-oriented rewards, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the OOD URSA-expert-2026 benchmark. Further analysis of reaction uniqueness shows that LLMs and conventional models explore complementary reaction spaces, motivating ensemble-based retrosynthesis systems. Overall, our results establish Top-K, plausibility-aware training as a practical new direction for robust future LLM-based synthesis planning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Top-K prompting for retrosynthesis to capture diverse plausible reactions, trains C3LM on a large dataset of ~45.6M verified reactions, and achieves SOTA performance on OOD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current single-answer evaluation protocols poorly capture the intrinsically one-to-many nature of retrosynthesis, which requires predicting diverse plausible reactions rather than just one correct answer.
AI.method: Introduces Top-K prompting as training/inference paradigm, compiles CREED-CCV-2+USPTO-XL dataset (~45.6M reactions), trains C3LM with constraint consistency, and integrates fine-tuning with ChemCensor-based and novelty-oriented rewards.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on the OOD URSA-expert-2026 benchmark. Analysis shows LLMs and conventional models explore complementary reaction spaces, suggesting ensemble approaches could be beneficial.
AI.conclusion: Top-K plausibility-aware training establishes a practical new direction for robust LLM-based synthesis planning, with potential for ensemble systems combining LLMs and conventional models.

title: Fuzzy Accuracy Compensates for Label Subjectivity in Classification of Skin Tone Using Wearable Photoplethysmography Signals
comment: This work was presented at the IEEE International Conference on Fuzzy Systems (FUZZ-IEEE) 2026
summary: We consider the problem of classification of skin tone using photoplethysmography (PPG) signals with labels of the ordinal six-class Fitzpatrick skin tones. A typical accuracy for this task is a poor 40-55 %. However, the labels are subjectively determined by comparing the skin with a colour chart, and hence contain widespread small-scale inaccuracies. By working with a "fuzzy accuracy", which deems a prediction of skin tone class to be correct if its difference from the labelled class is not greater than one, much higher accuracy is obtained which provides more convincing evidence that skin tone can be accurately predicted from PPG signals. Three machine learning approaches were used, namely deep learning or tree-based approaches on raw PPG signals, deep learning on image representations of the signals generated by the Symmetric Projection Attractor Reconstruction (SPAR) method, and machine learning on features extracted from the signals. The first method also employed a fuzzy version of the cross entropy loss function, which gave the best results. Tree-based models on raw signals give accuracies up to 55 % and higher fuzzy accuracies up to 96 %, while deep learning models on the SPAR images obtained lower results of 44 % accuracy and 85 % fuzzy accuracy. The machine learning on PPG features gave similar results to the SPAR method with accuracy of 42 % and fuzzy accuracy of 87 %. We have shown that classification of skin tone using PPG signals is possible with high fuzzy accuracy which implies that our modelling approach enables accurate prediction of skin tone class within at most one class of the observer's choice of class, from which we conclude that PPG signals are affected by skin tone in a discernible way.

AI.tldr: Skin tone classification using PPG signals achieves poor 40-55% accuracy with ordinal Fitzpatrick classes, but using "fuzzy accuracy" (prediction within ±1 class) yields much higher 85-96% accuracy, showing PPG signals contain skin tone information.
AI.motivation: Standard skin tone classification using PPG signals shows poor accuracy (40-55%), but these labels are subjective and contain small-scale inaccuracies since they're determined by comparing skin to color charts. The researchers wanted to better assess whether PPG signals actually contain meaningful skin tone information despite labeling imperfections.
AI.method: Three machine learning approaches: 1) Deep learning or tree-based models on raw PPG signals with fuzzy cross entropy loss, 2) Deep learning on SPAR (Symmetric Projection Attractor Reconstruction) image representations of signals, and 3) Machine learning on features extracted from PPG signals. They introduced "fuzzy accuracy" where predictions within ±1 class are considered correct.
AI.result: Tree-based models on raw signals achieved up to 55% standard accuracy and 96% fuzzy accuracy. Deep learning on SPAR images obtained 44% accuracy and 85% fuzzy accuracy. Feature-based ML gave 42% accuracy and 87% fuzzy accuracy. Fuzzy cross entropy loss with tree models gave best results.
AI.conclusion: PPG signals can classify skin tone with high fuzzy accuracy (predicting within one class of observer's choice), demonstrating that PPG signals are affected by skin tone in a discernible way, despite the subjectivity of Fitzpatrick scale labeling.

title: Monroe: A Molecular Foundation Model for In-Context Probabilistic Inference
comment: Preprint; Open source weights and code
summary: Bioassay activity prediction is often data-limited because drug-discovery datasets rely on time-consuming and expensive wet-lab experiments for data generation and evaluation. This challenge has inspired recent research into molecular foundation models (MFMs), which aim to encode general-purpose chemical knowledge into molecular representations that generalize well in data-constrained scenarios. This paper presents Monroe, a new MFM with several innovations over the existing state of the art: increased scale allowing pre-training on over 81 million molecules from the PM6 quantum chemistry dataset; improved graph representation of stereochemistry; improved training losses including conformer denoising and embedding decorrelation; improved multi-task learning; and the use of a prior-data-fitted model (TabPFN) for downstream in-context prediction. Our evaluations use a principled pairwise comparison framework that measures statistically significant performance differences. Across established Polaris benchmarks, Monroe matches or exceeds existing MFMs, while on activity cliff benchmarks, designed to assess utility for molecular discovery, it achieves significant improvements over prior methods. Finally, ablation and transfer experiments show that PFN-based downstream predictors also substantially improve two leading existing models, MiniMol and CheMeleon, yielding new state-of-the-art variants we call MiniMol_PFN and CheMeleon_PFN, suggesting that our downstream adaptation strategy generalizes beyond Monroe. Source code is at github.com/blazejba/monroe.

AI.tldr: Monroe is a new molecular foundation model that introduces several innovations including larger-scale pre-training, improved stereochemistry representation, enhanced training losses, and a novel downstream prediction strategy using TabPFN, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Bioassay activity prediction faces data limitations due to expensive and time-consuming wet-lab experiments. Existing approaches struggle in data-constrained scenarios, creating a need for molecular foundation models that can encode general-purpose chemical knowledge and generalize well with limited data.
AI.method: Monroe introduces several innovations: 1) Increased scale with pre-training on over 81 million molecules from PM6 quantum chemistry dataset, 2) Improved graph representation of stereochemistry, 3) Enhanced training losses including conformer denoising and embedding decorrelation, 4) Improved multi-task learning, and 5) Use of TabPFN (a prior-data-fitted model) for downstream in-context prediction.
AI.result: Monroe matches or exceeds existing molecular foundation models on established Polaris benchmarks and achieves significant improvements on activity cliff benchmarks. The TabPFN-based downstream predictors also substantially improve two leading existing models (MiniMol and CheMeleon), creating new state-of-the-art variants MiniMol_PFN and CheMeleon_PFN.
AI.conclusion: Monroe represents a significant advancement in molecular foundation models, with innovations in scale, representation, and downstream adaptation that deliver superior performance. The TabPFN-based downstream prediction strategy generalizes well to other models, suggesting broader applicability beyond Monroe itself.

title: Harness Continual Learning: Continual Adaptation Beyond Model Parameters
summary: Continual learning has largely been model-centric, treating model parameters as the state that changes with sequential experience. Modern agents can also adapt through a harness of prompts, memories, tools, skills, and routing rules. Because these contents jointly shape later execution, a harness update can disrupt previously reliable behavior even when the model is frozen. This raises a new question: how can an agent continually improve its state outside the model while retaining behavior acquired earlier? We formulate Harness Continual Learning (HCL), a new continual learning paradigm in which the harness evolves around a frozen foundation model, and define the resulting loss of earlier behavior as harness-level forgetting. We instantiate HCL with four execution-facing components: the Task Interface, Experience Memory, Capability Map, and Adaptive Router. We further introduce guarded harness evolution to separate update generation from state commitment. A Continual Optimizer proposes candidate harnesses from post-execution feedback, and a Continual Evaluator commits the resulting candidate harness only after checking current improvement, historical retention, and validity. Experiments on textual reasoning, multimodal perception, and open-world interaction demonstrate capability accumulation and failure recovery, with relative gains exceeding 10% over corresponding baselines in multiple settings. Component ablations assess the contribution of each harness component, while controlled retention sweeps reveal measurable harness-level forgetting and show that the stability--plasticity trade-off can be explicitly adjusted.

AI.tldr: A new continual learning paradigm called Harness Continual Learning (HCL) focuses on evolving the agent's harness (prompts, memories, tools, skills, routing rules) around a frozen foundation model while preventing disruption of previously learned behaviors.
AI.motivation: Traditional continual learning is model-centric, focusing on updating model parameters, but modern agents adapt through various harness components. When these harness components are updated, they can disrupt previously reliable behaviors even when the model is frozen, creating a new problem of harness-level forgetting.
AI.method: Proposes HCL paradigm with four execution-facing harness components: Task Interface, Experience Memory, Capability Map, and Adaptive Router. Introduces guarded harness evolution with a Continual Optimizer that proposes harness updates from feedback, and a Continual Evaluator that commits updates only after checking for improvement, historical retention, and validity.
AI.result: Experiments on textual reasoning, multimodal perception, and open-world interaction show capability accumulation and failure recovery, with relative gains exceeding 10% over baselines. Component ablations assess each harness component's contribution, and retention sweeps reveal measurable harness-level forgetting and adjustable stability-plasticity trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Harness Continual Learning provides a systematic framework for agents to continually improve their harness components while preserving earlier learned behaviors, addressing harness-level forgetting and enabling explicit adjustment of the stability-plasticity trade-off in continual learning systems.

title: Multi-Agent Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning for Smart Campus Coverage
summary: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has recently gained a great attention due to its real-time adaptation and effectiveness in complex optimization problems. This paper investigates the optimal deployment of millimeter-wave (mmWave) base stations (BSs) in a realistic, non-convex campus topology. The optimization problem is NP-hard, due to the non-convex, non-smooth nature of the max-min fairness objective. To overcome these constraints, we formulate the BS placement as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and systematically benchmark four DRL schemes: a discrete single-agent Deep Q-Network (DQN), a spatially partitioned Multi-Agent DQN, a continuous single-agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG), and a geographically partitioned multi-agent DDPG framework. Numerical evaluations reveal that the multi-agent DDPG approach substantially outperforms single-agent in dense scenarios. Additionally full coverage is achieved, and a fairness Jain's index of 0.94 is obtained. Finally, the multi-agent demonstrates highly efficient computational convergence of dense scenarios with $400$ users.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent DDPG achieves optimal mmWave BS deployment with full coverage and high fairness in dense campus scenarios.
AI.motivation: mmWave BS deployment in realistic non-convex campus topologies is NP-hard due to max-min fairness optimization with non-convex, non-smooth objectives, requiring effective solutions.
AI.method: Formulate BS placement as MDP and benchmark four DRL schemes: discrete single-agent DQN, spatially partitioned Multi-Agent DQN, continuous single-agent DDPG, and geographically partitioned multi-agent DDPG.
AI.result: Multi-agent DDPG substantially outperforms single-agent in dense scenarios, achieves full coverage, obtains Jain's fairness index of 0.94, and demonstrates efficient computational convergence with 400 users.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent DRL, particularly geographically partitioned DDPG, provides an effective solution for optimal mmWave BS deployment in complex campus environments with superior performance in dense scenarios.

title: Does Mapping Non-Maximal Probabilities to GMM Components Matter for S-JEPA Encoder Representations?
summary: S-JEPA uses soft Gaussian mixture model (GMM) posteriors instead of hard cluster labels to preserve uncertainty. It remains unclear whether the probability values alone are sufficient, or whether it also matters which GMM components receive the non-maximal probabilities. We test this with two matched controls. FIXED-RANDPERM keeps the top-1 component and probability together with the multiset of non-maximal probability values, but reassigns those non-maximal values using a mapping fixed for each physical frame. UNIFORM-TAIL keeps the top-1 component, its probability, and total non-maximal mass but distributes that mass uniformly. Across three independent seeds, REAL SOFT outperforms both controls on two frozen Encoder readouts. It provides better recovery of the original GMM tail and greater accessibility of spectral dynamics over short time scales after controlling for the complete spectrum of the current frame. In two exposure experiments, both readouts improved overall as more frames retained the original mapping. We also descriptively follow one Phase 2 trajectory after the switch to the online GMM. These results show that the numerical probability structure of the soft target does not fully determine the learned Encoder representation. The mapping of non-maximal probabilities to GMM components also matters.

AI.tldr: The study investigates whether the mapping of non-maximal probabilities to specific GMM components matters in soft JEPA learning, or if probability values alone are sufficient.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses uncertainty in whether probability values alone are sufficient for learning in S-JEPA's soft GMM posteriors, or whether the specific mapping of non-maximal probabilities to GMM components also matters.
AI.method: The researchers test two matched controls against REAL SOFT: FIXED-RANDPERM (preserves top-1 component and probability values but reassigns non-maximal values with fixed mapping) and UNIFORM-TAIL (keeps top-1 component but distributes non-maximal mass uniformly). They use three independent seeds and evaluate on frozen Encoder readouts, with additional exposure experiments and Phase 2 trajectory analysis.
AI.result: REAL SOFT outperforms both controls on two frozen Encoder readouts, showing better recovery of original GMM tail and greater accessibility of spectral dynamics over short time scales. Both readouts improved overall as more frames retained original mapping in exposure experiments.
AI.conclusion: The numerical probability structure of soft targets does not fully determine learned Encoder representations - the specific mapping of non-maximal probabilities to GMM components also matters for representation quality.

title: Open-MOPD: Diagnosing and Fixing Capability Imbalance in Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for consolidating domain-specialized reinforcement learning (RL) experts into a single generalist student via dense, token-level reward supervision. Despite its practical success, the optimization dynamics governing multi-teacher capability integration remain poorly understood, and open, rigorously reproducible recipes are conspicuously lacking. In this work, we establish a controlled M-OPD benchmark on SmolLM3-3B-Base with oracle routing, isolating capability integration from routing ambiguity. Our investigation reveals a pronounced capability integration gap: standard M-OPD captures only 35.6% of the available headroom relative to a domain-routed oracle ensemble, with concise tasks such as instruction following suffering severe degradation and premature stagnation. Crucially, we show that this failure stems not from gradient conflict, but from a severe misallocation of the token-level optimization budget. This pathology is driven by three orthogonal factors: structural sequence-length disparities across domains, dynamic convergence drift due to non-uniform learning rates, and multi-step reward staleness from asynchronous policy updates. To resolve these imbalances, we introduce Open-MOPD, a principled framework incorporating token-share balancing, gap-aware dynamic budget allocation, and student reward refresh. Together, these mechanisms systematically restore cross-domain balance, elevating headroom recovery from 35.6% to 83.4% in a single deployable student. We fully open-source our end-to-end post-training recipe, training trajectories, and evaluation suites on an academically accessible hardware budget.

AI.tldr: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD) for RL experts is improved through Open-MOPD framework with token-share balancing, gap-aware dynamic budget allocation, and student reward refresh, recovering 83.4% of oracle ensemble performance vs 35.6% baseline.
AI.motivation: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation has shown promise for consolidating domain-specialized RL experts into a generalist student, but suffers from poor optimization dynamics understanding and lack of reproducible recipes. There's a significant capability integration gap where standard M-OPD captures only 35.6% of available performance headroom.
AI.method: Established controlled M-OPD benchmark on SmolLM3-3B-Base with oracle routing to isolate capability integration. Introduced Open-MOPD framework with three key mechanisms: token-share balancing to address structural sequence-length disparities, gap-aware dynamic budget allocation to handle dynamic convergence drift, and student reward refresh to mitigate multi-step reward staleness.
AI.result: Open-MOPD elevates headroom recovery from 35.6% to 83.4% relative to domain-routed oracle ensemble. The framework successfully addresses the identified pathologies stemming from token-level optimization budget misallocation rather than gradient conflict.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a principled solution to multi-teacher capability integration in RL distillation through Open-MOPD, offering systematic mechanisms to restore cross-domain balance. The work includes fully open-sourced post-training recipes, training trajectories, and evaluation suites on accessible hardware.

title: Pretraining Reusable Inference Across Views with Synthetic Task Priors
summary: Modern pretrained encoders make representations from heterogeneous views increasingly reusable, but the procedure that determines view utility and combines evidence is still relearned for each downstream task. Consequently, knowledge about view relevance, complementarity, reliability, and missingness is repeatedly discarded rather than transferred across tasks. We therefore reformulate multi-view learning as learning a reusable, task-conditioned inference procedure rather than a fixed fusion function. Based on this perspective, we propose SIMPLE, a prior-fitted multi-view in-context learner that predicts query labels by conditioning on a small labeled support set. Since existing real-world datasets cover only a limited range of view configurations and task structures, we construct a controllable synthetic task prior in embedding space. It generates diverse support-query episodes with varying class structures, shared and view-specific factors, representation geometries, cross-view dependencies, reliability levels, missingness patterns, and distribution shifts. A hierarchical inference architecture then performs reasoning within views, across views, and across support and query samples. Experiments on multi-view and multi-omics benchmarks demonstrate that the frozen variant of SIMPLE achieves competitive performance without updating the inference backbone, while lightweight adapter calibration attains leading performance on most evaluated datasets. Together, the results under frozen, one-shot, and missing-view settings support the central hypothesis that multi-view reasoning itself can be pretrained and reused, while lightweight adapter calibration provides task-specific alignment when needed.

AI.tldr: SIMPLE learns reusable multi-view reasoning through in-context learning with a synthetic task prior, enabling transferable inference across tasks without full retraining.
AI.motivation: Current multi-view learning systems relearn fusion procedures for each downstream task, discarding valuable knowledge about view relevance, complementarity, reliability, and missingness across tasks, preventing knowledge transfer.
AI.method: Proposes SIMPLE: a prior-fitted multi-view in-context learner that predicts query labels by conditioning on labeled support sets. Uses a controllable synthetic task prior in embedding space to generate diverse episodes covering various view configurations and task structures, with hierarchical inference architecture for within-view, cross-view, and support-query reasoning.
AI.result: Frozen SIMPLE achieves competitive performance without updating inference backbone; lightweight adapter calibration attains leading performance on most evaluated multi-view and multi-omics benchmarks. Works well under frozen, one-shot, and missing-view settings.
AI.conclusion: Multi-view reasoning can be pretrained and reused across tasks, with lightweight adapter calibration providing task-specific alignment when needed, enabling transferable knowledge about view properties while avoiding full task-specific retraining.

title: Enhancing EBSD throughput of battery electrode materials using super-resolution generative adversarial networks
summary: Quantitative microstructural characterization of Li-ion battery electrode materials using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) has been proven as a critical method for optimizing cell performance. However, the inherently slow nature of EBSD can hinder the throughput of analyses needed for statistical representation of a material microstructure being developed. This work demonstrates a machine learning super-resolution framework using a generative adversarial network (SRGAN) to significantly increase EBSD throughput. The SRGAN model was trained on EBSD data of LiNixMnyCozO2 (NMC) cathode particles to computationally enhance low-resolution datasets and its performance is compared against classical interpolation methods across various upscaling factors (2x to 12x). Both qualitative image metrics and quantitative microstructural analysis verified that the SRGAN systematically outperformed classical methods, particularly in preserving small grains and maintaining realistic grain boundaries. We demonstrate that a 5x upscaling factor, corresponding to a 25x speed-up in acquisition time or a 25x larger field of view, is practical while maintaining acceptable accuracy in key metrics like grain size and shape. For instance, at 5x upscaling, relative errors were +5.7%, +8.2%, and -14.6% on grain area-equivalent diameter, grain maximum sphere-inscribed diameter, and grain boundary length, respectively. The SRGAN methodology developed in this work significantly enhances the efficiency of EBSD acquisition for more statistically robust microstructural dataset, enabling EBSD as a high-throughput characterization tool for materials research and industrial process development.

AI.tldr: A machine learning super-resolution framework (SRGAN) significantly increases EBSD throughput for Li-ion battery electrode characterization by computationally enhancing low-resolution datasets with up to 25x speed-up while maintaining acceptable accuracy.
AI.motivation: EBSD is crucial for Li-ion battery electrode optimization but inherently slow, hindering statistical representation of microstructure needed for material development. There's a need to increase analysis throughput while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: Developed a machine learning super-resolution framework using a generative adversarial network (SRGAN) trained on EBSD data of NMC cathode particles. The model computationally enhances low-resolution datasets and compares performance against classical interpolation methods across various upscaling factors (2x to 12x).
AI.result: SRGAN systematically outperformed classical methods in preserving small grains and maintaining realistic grain boundaries. A 5x upscaling factor provides practical benefits: 25x speed-up in acquisition time or 25x larger field of view while maintaining acceptable accuracy. At 5x upscaling, relative errors were +5.7% (grain diameter), +8.2% (sphere-inscribed diameter), and -14.6% (grain boundary length).
AI.conclusion: The SRGAN methodology significantly enhances EBSD efficiency, enabling more statistically robust microstructural datasets and transforming EBSD into a high-throughput characterization tool for materials research and industrial process development.

title: Discretizing Continuous Time Series for Imputation with Masked Diffusion Training
summary: Time series imputation is a crucial area for reliable time series analysis, yet it remains challenging due to the complex temporal dynamics and noise of real-world data. Existing approaches, however, exhibit two limitations: missing and observed values are embedded within the same representation space without explicit structural separation, and continuous diffusion-based methods are trained to predict added noise rather than the original signal. To address these, we propose the Masked Diffusion Time-series Imputation Model (MDTIM), which leverages the training paradigm of masked diffusion model for imputation tasks. The MASK token is structurally orthogonal to valid observations, and the model directly predicts the original values, naturally aligning both the representation and the learning objective with the imputation task. To bridge the gap between discrete masked diffusion and the continuous, ordinal nature of time series, we further introduce Stochastic Discretization, which maps continuous values to ordinal-aware tokens while preserving continuous dynamics. Our experiments on diverse benchmarks confirm that MDTIM achieves superior robustness and scalability, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art deterministic and generative baselines across various missing scenarios.

AI.tldr: Masked Diffusion Time-series Imputation Model (MDTIM) uses a masked diffusion approach with structural separation between missing and observed values, directly predicting original signals rather than noise, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Time series imputation is crucial but challenging due to complex temporal dynamics and noise. Existing approaches have two key limitations: (1) missing and observed values are embedded in the same representation space without structural separation, and (2) continuous diffusion methods are trained to predict added noise rather than the original signal.
AI.method: Proposes MDTIM with masked diffusion training paradigm for imputation. Uses MASK token structurally orthogonal to valid observations. Introduces Stochastic Discretization to bridge gap between discrete masked diffusion and continuous ordinal nature of time series, mapping continuous values to ordinal-aware tokens while preserving dynamics.
AI.result: MDTIM achieves superior robustness and scalability on diverse benchmarks, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art deterministic and generative baselines across various missing scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The masked diffusion approach with structural separation and direct signal prediction naturally aligns representation and learning objectives with imputation tasks, providing an effective solution for time series imputation.

title: PGFS++: Molecular Property Improvement under Synthesis and Diversity Constraints
summary: Improving molecular properties, such as drug-likeness or binding affinity, is a recurring task in early-stage drug discovery. However, molecules optimized in an unconstrained chemical space have limited practical value if they cannot be synthesized. Policy Gradient for Forward Synthesis (PGFS) is a synthesis-aware reinforcement learning method for molecular improvement, but its use of reactant embedding prediction makes reactant selection indirect, which, as we show, limits learning effectiveness. We first develop PGFS+, in which reaction templates and second reactants are represented by trainable embedding lookup tables. Combined with a more effective scoring function and RL algorithm, PGFS+ significantly improves the desired property. However, it exposes a reward-hacking failure mode: a powerful reactant search can map diverse input molecules to the same high-reward magnet molecule, improving the reward while collapsing the output diversity. We therefore introduce PGFS++, a synthesis-aware reinforcement learning framework for input-specific molecular improvement. Given an input molecule, PGFS++ treats it as the start of a forward-synthesis trajectory, applies learned reaction templates with compatible in-stock building blocks, and produces a molecule with improved target properties, an explicit synthesis route, and structural similarity to the input. Experiments on molecular improvement tasks show that PGFS++ improves target properties while preserving high output diversity.

AI.tldr: PGFS++ is a synthesis-aware RL framework that improves molecular properties while maintaining diversity and providing explicit synthesis routes, addressing reward hacking in previous approaches.
AI.motivation: Improving molecular properties like drug-likeness or binding affinity is crucial in early drug discovery, but unconstrained optimization often produces molecules that are difficult or impossible to synthesize, limiting practical value. Previous synthesis-aware RL methods (PGFS) had limitations in learning effectiveness due to indirect reactant selection.
AI.method: PGFS++ treats input molecules as starting points for forward-synthesis trajectories, applying learned reaction templates with compatible in-stock building blocks. It uses trainable embedding lookup tables for reaction templates and second reactants, combined with improved scoring functions and RL algorithms. The framework specifically addresses reward hacking by ensuring input-specific improvements rather than mapping diverse inputs to the same high-reward molecules.
AI.result: Experiments on molecular improvement tasks show that PGFS++ successfully improves target properties while preserving high output diversity, unlike previous versions that suffered from reward-hacking where diverse inputs were mapped to the same "magnet" molecules, collapsing diversity.
AI.conclusion: PGFS++ provides an effective synthesis-aware reinforcement learning framework for molecular improvement that maintains structural similarity to input molecules, preserves output diversity, and provides explicit synthesis routes, addressing key limitations of previous approaches while achieving better property optimization.

title: Leaf Values as Coordinates: Exact Contrastive Explanation for Gradient-Boosted Ensembles
summary:
A gradient-boosted ensemble predicts by summing one leaf value per tree. Read
  those values as coordinates rather than as intermediate results, and every
  instance becomes a point in R^M on which the model acts linearly: the score is
  the sum of the coordinates.
  This small change of view makes contrastive explanation exact. The difference
  between two instances is a vector that is identically zero wherever they share
  a leaf, so the gap between a rejected applicant and an accepted one is carried
  by a handful of coordinates, each traceable to a real split in a real tree.
  Nothing is fitted, sampled, or assumed additive in features -- the additivity
  is already there, in the right space.
  We build a recourse method on this representation and evaluate it on five
  tabular datasets under repeated cross-validation. Its recommendation
  reconstructs the model's own decision to 6.2 x 10^-15, so an auditor can
  re-check the arithmetic without the model. On the credit datasets it is
  Pareto-non-dominated on effort against realism. And when recommendations are
  restricted to changes the subject could actually make -- not their age, not a
  settled delinquency -- it retains 58% of its validity where the strongest
  baseline retains 41%, a distinction the standard evaluation cannot see because
  it never asks whether a recommendation can be carried out.

AI.tldr: Gradient boosting models can be reinterpreted as linear operations on leaf coordinate space, enabling exact contrastive explanations and recourse recommendations that are mathematically precise and practically actionable.
AI.motivation: Existing explanation methods for gradient-boosted ensembles often rely on approximations, sampling, or feature additivity assumptions. The paper aims to provide exact explanations without additional fitting, sampling, or additive assumptions by leveraging the inherent structure of gradient boosting models.
AI.method: Reinterprets gradient-boosted ensemble predictions as linear operations in R^M space where each tree's leaf value becomes a coordinate. This representation enables exact contrastive explanations by analyzing vector differences between instances. The method traces differences directly to specific tree splits without additional computation.
AI.result: The exact representation achieves reconstruction error of 6.2×10^-15 (essentially perfect). On credit datasets, recommendations are Pareto-non-dominated on effort vs realism. When restricted to actionable changes (excluding immutable attributes like age), the method retains 58% validity vs 41% for strongest baseline, revealing limitations of standard evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Gradient boosting models inherently operate linearly in leaf coordinate space, enabling exact explanations and recourse recommendations. This perspective reveals that standard evaluations overlook practical actionability of recommendations, and the proposed method provides mathematically precise explanations without additional computational overhead.

title: Beyond Trial Averaging: Anchoring Neural and Visual Representations for Few-Repetition Brain-to-Image Retrieval
summary: Decoding visual information from brain signals probes neural representations and enables neuro-rehabilitation and dream decoding. Recent brain-to-image retrieval approaches have achieved promising performance, typically by averaging many (up to 80) neural trials per image, requiring repeated stimulus presentation that increases latency, cost, and user burden. When only one or a few repetitions are available, the retrieval accuracy drops sharply. This drop is commonly attributed to query noise because averaging suppresses noise and increases signal stability. However, we find a non-transitive alignment pattern: the low-repetition query signal and the image representation each align with the high-repetition center, but not directly with each other. This pattern shows that query noise is only part of the problem and that gallery placement also affects retrieval. We therefore propose a neural-anchor-based retrieval (NEAR) framework that treats the high-repetition center as an anchor and approaches it from both sides: a denoiser pulls the noisy query toward the true anchor, and a small network predicts each candidate's pseudo anchor from its image and pulls the image toward it. Across four datasets spanning EEG, MEG and fMRI, NEAR consistently improved retrieval in the few-repetition regime. On THINGS-EEG2, it improved 200-way Top-1 accuracy by 5.7 and 9.3 percentage points respectively, when averaging one and four repetitions. By anchoring neural and visual representations, NEAR reduces reliance on repeated acquisition and brings neural retrieval closer to real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: NEAR is a neural-anchor-based retrieval framework that improves brain-to-image retrieval with few neural repetitions by using high-repetition centers as anchors and aligning both noisy queries and image representations toward these anchors.
AI.motivation: Current brain-to-image retrieval approaches require averaging many neural trials per image (up to 80 repetitions), which increases latency, cost, and user burden. When only one or few repetitions are available, accuracy drops sharply. The problem isn't just query noise - gallery placement also affects retrieval due to a non-transitive alignment pattern where low-repetition queries and image representations both align with high-repetition centers but not directly with each other.
AI.method: NEAR uses high-repetition centers as anchors and approaches them from both sides: (1) a denoiser pulls the noisy query toward the true anchor, and (2) a small network predicts each candidate's pseudo anchor from its image and pulls the image representation toward it. This framework aligns both neural and visual representations with the anchor points.
AI.result: NEAR consistently improved retrieval in the few-repetition regime across four datasets spanning EEG, MEG, and fMRI. On THINGS-EEG2, it improved 200-way Top-1 accuracy by 5.7 and 9.3 percentage points respectively when averaging one and four repetitions.
AI.conclusion: By anchoring neural and visual representations, NEAR reduces reliance on repeated neural acquisition and brings brain-to-image retrieval closer to real-world deployment, addressing both query noise and gallery placement issues in few-repetition scenarios.

title: SCORE: Subject Coordinate Recovery for Label-Free Cross-Subject EEG-to-Image Retrieval
summary: Accurate visual decoding can reveal how the brain represents visual information and recover perceived content from neural signals such as electroencephalography (EEG), with potential for neural communication. However, current EEG-to-image retrieval methods perform far below their within-subject counterparts for new users without labeled calibration, limiting real-world deployment. To understand this gap, we analyze EEG features across subjects and find that different subjects preserve similar relationships among concepts but express them along different coordinate directions. We therefore propose Subject Coordinate Recovery (SCORE), a target label-free framework combining recovery-aware source training with coordinate alignment at deployment. During training, SCORE aligns source subject EEG with a common image space and simulates unseen-subject recovery through source-only episodes. At deployment, with both encoders frozen, SCORE selects reliable EEG-image landmarks through hubness-corrected matching and estimates an orthogonal transformation to recover target EEG coordinates without source data or target labels. In 200-way retrieval on two public benchmarks, SCORE outperforms the unadapted baseline for every target subject and achieves the best overall accuracy. It reaches 53.23%/83.55% and 12.01%/32.16% Top-1/Top-5 on THINGS-EEG2 and Alljoined-1.6M, respectively, surpassing the strongest baselines by 17.45/15.70 and 3.08/4.62 percentage points. Without target labels or encoder updates, SCORE brings brain-based visual decoding closer to robust, practical, low-latency deployment across users.

AI.tldr: SCORE is a subject coordinate recovery framework for EEG-to-image retrieval that enables cross-subject visual decoding without target labels or calibration data.
AI.motivation: Current EEG-to-image retrieval methods perform poorly for new users without labeled calibration data, limiting real-world deployment of brain-based visual decoding systems.
AI.method: Proposes Subject Coordinate Recovery (SCORE) - a target label-free framework with recovery-aware source training and coordinate alignment. During training, aligns source EEG with common image space and simulates unseen-subject recovery. At deployment, selects EEG-image landmarks using hubness-corrected matching and estimates orthogonal transformation to recover target coordinates.
AI.result: Achieves 53.23%/83.55% Top-1/Top-5 on THINGS-EEG2 and 12.01%/32.16% on Alljoined-1.6M in 200-way retrieval, outperforming all baselines by significant margins (17.45/15.70 and 3.08/4.62 percentage points).
AI.conclusion: SCORE enables robust, practical, low-latency cross-subject EEG-to-image retrieval without target labels or encoder updates, advancing brain-based visual decoding toward real-world deployment.

title: Bridge Graphical Models: Coupling, Projection, and Current-Preserving Dynamics for Generative Modeling
summary: Continuous-time generative models are often built from endpoint-conditioned bridges, but generation requires a different object: a non-anticipative Markov decoder that only observes the current state and time. We identify this bridge-to-decoder compression as a structural bottleneck shared by diffusion models, flow matching, rectified flow, Schrödinger bridges, and field-based generative models. We introduce the \emph{Markovization gap}, the time-integrated conditional variance of the bridge velocity given the Markov state. It is the MMSE of predicting endpoint-conditioned motion from the information available to a sampler, and it measures an irreducible loss incurred before any neural network is trained. To make this bottleneck comparable across model families, we define \emph{Bridge Graphical Models} (BGMs), which separate endpoint coupling, bridge law, Markovian projection, and current-preserving dynamics representation as independent design choices. The same formalism also represents Poisson and electrostatic models as field-line bridge kernels with a corresponding field-line Markovization gap. Across synthetic, latent, and pixel-space pilots on CIFAR-10 and Fashion-MNIST, a feature-space proxy gap estimated in minutes before training ranks design choices in the same direction as downstream training loss and FID under fixed architecture, bridge, sampler, and compute. These results support the Markovization gap as a pre-training diagnostic for bridge and coupling design.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a "Markovization gap" as a structural bottleneck in continuous-time generative models and introduces Bridge Graphical Models (BGMs) to compare this bottleneck across different model families.
AI.motivation: Continuous-time generative models are built from endpoint-conditioned bridges, but generation requires non-anticipative Markov decoders. There's a fundamental gap between these two representations that acts as a structural bottleneck shared by various generative modeling approaches.
AI.method: 1) Introduces the "Markovization gap" - the time-integrated conditional variance of bridge velocity given Markov state. 2) Defines Bridge Graphical Models (BGMs) to separate endpoint coupling, bridge law, Markovian projection, and dynamics representation as independent design choices. 3) Extends formalism to represent Poisson and electrostatic models. 4) Validates using feature-space proxy gap estimated before training on synthetic, latent, and pixel-space datasets.
AI.result: Across CIFAR-10 and Fashion-MNIST experiments, the pre-training feature-space proxy gap ranks design choices consistently with downstream training loss and FID under fixed architecture and compute. The Markovization gap serves as an effective pre-training diagnostic.
AI.conclusion: The Markovization gap represents an irreducible loss in continuous-time generative models before neural network training, and Bridge Graphical Models provide a unified framework to compare this bottleneck across different model families. The gap can be used as a pre-training diagnostic for bridge and coupling design.

title: Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning for Controlled Hawkes Jump-Diffusions
summary: We study stochastic control of multivariate Hawkes-driven stochastic differential equations with machine learning algorithms in a non-Markovian setting. Due to the path dependence of the memory of the Hawkes intensity, this problem does not fall within classical stochastic control theory outside particular Markovian kernels. We first develop a finite-dimensional Markovianization procedure and algorithm to approximate multivariate Hawkes processes with mixtures of exponential kernels. We prove the convergence of the Markovianized approximation of the Hawkes process, its intensity, and the value of the problem to the original non-Markovian processes and the value of the primal problem. We then formulate continuous-time deterministic policy gradient learning on the Markovianized approximation of the problem, called Hawkes-CT DDPG. We propose a model-free algorithm to solve the non-Markovian Hawkes-driven optimization by observing only the event times of the process, the realization of the solution to the SDE, and a chosen set of decay filters, while the Hawkes kernel coefficients remain unknown. We compare our continuous time reinforcement learning Hawkes-CT DDPG method with discrete time reinforcement learning techniques under three different types of kernels: simple exponential, Erlang, and power-law kernels.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a machine learning approach for stochastic control of Hawkes-driven SDEs in non-Markovian settings by approximating Hawkes processes with mixtures of exponential kernels and applying continuous-time reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Classical stochastic control theory fails for multivariate Hawkes-driven SDEs in non-Markovian settings due to path-dependent memory in Hawkes intensity. Existing methods are limited to particular Markovian kernels, creating a need for more general solutions for this class of problems.
AI.method: 1) Develop a finite-dimensional Markovianization procedure to approximate multivariate Hawkes processes with mixtures of exponential kernels. 2) Formulate continuous-time deterministic policy gradient learning (Hawkes-CT DDPG) on the Markovianized approximation. 3) Propose a model-free algorithm that works with only observed event times, SDE realizations, and decay filters, without requiring known Hawkes kernel coefficients.
AI.result: The paper proves convergence of the Markovianized approximation of Hawkes processes, their intensity, and problem values to original non-Markovian processes. It demonstrates the Hawkes-CT DDPG method and compares it with discrete-time reinforcement learning techniques under exponential, Erlang, and power-law kernels.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully addresses stochastic control of non-Markovian Hawkes-driven SDEs through Markovianization and continuous-time reinforcement learning, providing a model-free solution that works without knowing Hawkes kernel coefficients and outperforms discrete-time methods across different kernel types.

title: Learned, Then Lost: A Measured Single-Example Counterfactual in Pre-training
summary: A single training example's contribution to a finished model is normally estimated rather than measured, because measuring it takes two expensive full pre-training runs that differ in one row of one batch. We ran that counterfactual 24 times at a small scale. We trained 32 GPT-2 models at 124M parameters from scratch on OpenWebText, over four conditions and eight seeds. At step 200 of 9,536, at peak learning rate, we replaced one row of a 256-row batch with a fixed context injection carrying a 194-token passage. The three injected conditions are: 1. fluent prose with a corpus-attested subject, 2. fluent prose with a fabricated subject matched to it within 0.14% on full-batch gradient delta, and 3. random keyboard characters. The fourth condition is an uninjected twin. The passage is learned from one exposure and then decays.
